item.title: The Context of the Crisis Facing Young Men
item.description:
Social Life

The Context of the Crisis Facing Young Men

Our survey aimed to get a handle on the challenges young men face, and their causes.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Young men are often described as languishing, with a harsh light turned on their struggles.
  • We developed a survey to hear from young men on these matters and explore common explanations.
  • The clearest source of trouble was the loss of institutional supports, such as predictable work trajectories.
Source: Roman Samborskyi/Shutterstock

Over the past 18 months, I joined with the Institute for Family Studies to conduct and report on a survey of 2,000 young men, ages 18-29. The survey was fielded in April 2025; Part I of the report was released in March 2026 and Part II in August 2026. In the conclusion to the report, I weighed some of the common explanations for why many men are languishing. In the adapted excerpt below, I consider the best account.

In the public discussion of young men, their struggles are often framed in a harsh “narrative” that goes like this: A growing number—too many—are failing in school, not working or studying, not dating or forming families, not leaving their childhood bedrooms. They are checked out from social life, have few, if any, friends, and belong to few, if any, social or civic groups. Their mental health is poor, their habits are bad—video games, pornography, gambling, pot-smoking—and their views are extremist.

As commonly told, the dark story of their failures is, at least implicitly, set against a more successful comparison group, whether young women or older generations of men.

To explain the crisis, writers and social scientists point to a few common causes, from unfavorable experiences in school to gaming addiction to the ill effects of “toxic masculinity.”

Of the possibilities, what we might call the “structural argument” is the one that finds the most support in our data.

The Structural Argument

In the common form of the structural argument, economic and educational changes are the most important contributing factors to the dire circumstances of young men. Among the detrimental changes are boy-unfriendly school policies, the loss of traditional male jobs, such as in manufacturing, and the decline of working-class men’s wages. Other shifts have increased the volatility of the economy, such as the rise of unstable gig work, disruptive new technologies, and now the looming threat of job loss due to artificial intelligence. As much evidence shows, alterations like these to the opportunity structure have been systematically disadvantageous to men.1

However, the loss of “structure” we discerned running through the survey responses also extends to wider issues. The social fabric itself has thinned—a deinstitutionalization, as sociologists call it, that has left our world more formless. Over time, there has been a sharp decline of prescribed roles, inherited life courses, clear occupational and educational trajectories, and the like. Where there was once a given social pattern—an “institution,” like sustained work for the same company—there is now a more open and indeterminate field of options and choices. Though ostensibly providing greater freedom, it is a precarious freedom, with less guidance from shared beliefs, customs, rules, or forms of life.

The Cost of Formlessness

We see what is lost by the importance of the college track. By nearly every metric, we find, men who took this route and stayed with it to graduation are faring the best. The benefit did not necessarily appear while they were in school, which could be a lonely, distressing time. Rather, it came afterward, when it opened doors or widened horizons to stable employment, friendships, marital partners, household establishment, community affiliation, and much else. These are the men most likely to feel they have reached full adulthood, and feel that they are not a failure or unwanted, and that they have some control over what happens to them.

But, we find, the higher-education pathway is not open to many men, including for financial reasons or family responsibilities, or because they are not interested or feel they will not succeed. Conditions that affect learning, like ADHD, autism, and dyslexia, are common among young men (about 25% of respondents report a current issue). Trade school or an apprenticeship program is clearly an option and a good one (15% have completed a program, with high employment), but we know from other studies that schools heavily stress college-for-all and are only now beginning to reintroduce shop class and talk about alternatives. In most situations, clearly defined non-college pathways or school-to-employer pipelines are missing.

In the current economic environment, where employment is now more fluid and uncertain, we find that attitudes toward work have changed. We find that many young men do not see a direct relationship between hard work and getting ahead. Rather, they appear to view things as more random, circumstantial, or indeterminate, such that, for instance, success is a matter of "who you know" (72% agreement) and “what happens to me is not under my control” (61%). Even half of college graduates doubt that their education was worth the time or money. Young men still retain a belief in their opportunities, yet how they expect to realize them might be better indicated by their extensive gambling and day-trading than by steady work in a 9-5 job. Even economists have taken to referring to the present situation as a “casino economy.”2

The lack of institutionalized social forms affects young men in many other personal ways. For example, with the long-running decline of voluntary associations—churches, service clubs, adult sports leagues, and the like—and the instability of the family (only about 60% of our respondents had the consistent presence of his father), young men are thrown back on themselves to find and create relationships of commitment and friendship. We show that while most unmarried or unpartnered young men want to date, it is rough sailing. Many cannot find someone who will go out with them (reported by about 50%) and—attesting to the more amorphous and fraught circumstances of courtship—are reluctant to ask a woman on a date, primarily out of fear of being turned down.

Those without institutional connections, without some community or church or school, are in the grimmest circumstances in terms of friendship and social integration. How, we might ask, are these men to form such relationships, when, “historically,” to quote two researchers, they “have been more the gifts of generational inheritance” than the result of some go-getter initiative?

They continue:

We inherit many overlapping webs of association … [and] the relationships we form through these shared associations—family, religion, community, place, or otherwise—beget new relationships and new associations. Contrary to the self-help ethos that pervades our society, relationships and community have never been solely individual choices to make nor individual responsibilities to develop.3

On these points and much else, we find social formlessness to be like a raging storm in which many young men are struggling to find some secure foothold.

item.title: The Corks in My Drawer: How to Give Up a Belief You Enjoyed Holding
item.description:
Cognitive Dissonance

The Corks in My Drawer: How to Give Up a Belief You Enjoyed Holding

Updating a belief and updating a behavior are separate events, often years apart.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Beliefs that grant permission get less scrutiny than beliefs that demand sacrifice.
  • The heart-healthy wine story rested on a molecule present in a glass at one-hundredth of the studied dose.
  • In 2001, 27 percent of Americans called moderate drinking bad for health. By 2026, half did.

I keep the corks. Douro, Montalcino, Etna, and a dozen others in a kitchen drawer with the twine and the batteries. My wife thinks the drawer is ridiculous. The drawer is a record of about 15 years of choosing where to go based on what grows there.

I'm also a physician who studies substance use, which means I spent those same 15 years reading the alcohol literature. I watched the heart-healthy wine story fall apart in slow motion, and I kept buying wine the entire time. The interesting part is not the science. The interesting part is the lag.

The story I inherited

In 1992, two French researchers published a paper in The Lancet naming the French Paradox: relatively low coronary disease in a country eating plenty of saturated fat. They pointed at wine. Morley Safer had already carried the idea into American living rooms on 60 Minutes in November 1991, and red wine sales in the United States rose 39 percent the following year. If you were an adult in the 1990s, you absorbed this whether or not you ever read a study.

The mechanism arrived next. Resveratrol, a compound in grape skins, got credited with the effect and became one of the most studied molecules in nutrition. The arithmetic never worked. A glass of red delivers less than two milligrams of resveratrol. Trials showing any effect used 100 to 500 milligrams a day. One dose-response analysis calculated you'd need roughly 111 glasses daily to reach the level studied for cancer prevention.

The founding laboratory result also came apart. In 2005, researchers showed resveratrol's apparent activation of the longevity enzyme SIRT1 depended on a fluorescent tag attached to the test molecule. Use the natural substrate, and the effect disappears. A 2025 review of 11 randomized trials found no change in human SIRT1 after supplementation at all. And one of the most prolific authors on resveratrol and heart protection, at the University of Connecticut, was found by investigators to have fabricated and falsified data across numerous papers, which triggered a wave of retractions.

Then the epidemiology went. The wine was never the problem. The comparison group was. A German cohort found 90.6 percent of people counted as abstainers were former drinkers, many of whom had quit because they were already sick. Line those people up against healthy moderate drinkers and wine looks protective without wine doing anything. When one team reanalyzed 87 studies correcting for this, the mortality benefit slid from a relative risk of 0.86 to 0.97, which is another way of saying the benefit vanished.

Why the belief held on

I knew about the sick-quitter critique years before I changed anything about how I talked or drank. Four things kept the belief alive in me:

  • The claim granted permission. Nearly all health advice asks you to give something up. This one handed something back. We scrutinize findings that demand sacrifice and wave through findings that license what we already do, and the asymmetry runs below conscious reasoning. I can tell you exactly which alcohol papers I read closely and which I skimmed, and the pattern is not flattering.
  • The belief was attached to identity. Wine, for me, means travel and long dinners and knowing why Etna tastes like ash. Question the health claim, and you brush against a self-concept. People defend identity-linked beliefs more stubbornly than ordinary ones and experience corrections as personal insult.
  • The story had machinery inside. A molecule, an enzyme, a pathway. A causal story feels more true than a bare correlation, even when the machinery explains nothing. Resveratrol made the French Paradox feel mechanistic rather than anecdotal, and the feeling survived long after the mechanism died.
  • The belief had social confirmation everywhere. Sommeliers repeated the claim. Physicians repeated the claim. My own father repeated the claim while pouring. Repetition by trusted people produces the same subjective certainty as evidence does, and the two are indistinguishable from the inside.

The country moved before I did

Gallup has asked Americans since 2001 whether moderate drinking harms health. In 2001, 27 percent said yes. In 2026, half do. That shift is one of the larger reversals in public health opinion in my lifetime, and most of the movement happened in the last four years.

Young adults got there first. Half of Americans aged 18 to 35 reported drinking in Gallup's 2025 survey, down from 59 percent in 2023. They came up after the 60 Minutes era and never received the permission the rest of us absorbed, which turns out to be an advantage: Nothing to unlearn.

What stays genuinely open

Wine drunk slowly, with food, spread across a week, might carry a small real benefit. A July 2026 analysis of two Spanish cohorts found lower mortality with moderate wine inside a Mediterranean diet, and the authors flagged that their analyses least vulnerable to the abstainer problem missed statistical significance. A Spanish trial is now randomizing 10,000 drinkers aged 50 to 75 to abstain or continue, the first real experiment in a field built almost entirely on observation. I'm not holding my breath, and I'm not pretending the question is closed either.

What changed for me

I still drink wine, but I have stopped calling wine healthy, out loud or in my head. The distinction matters to me, because "heart-healthy" was an argument for the second glass, and "I enjoy this" makes no argument at all. The second glass now has to justify itself, and sometimes it just doesn’t.

If you want the transferable version: Notice which studies you read carefully. Notice which ones you accept in a sentence. In the gap between those two habits hides a comfortable belief, and the gap is invisible from the inside unless you go looking for it.

The drawer is still full. I only added one in June.

item.title: Are Apologies Used Like Tylenol for Workplace Conflicts?
item.description:
Forgiveness

Are Apologies Used Like Tylenol for Workplace Conflicts?

Apologies offer temporary relief. True resolution requires structural changes.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Repeat apologies are symptoms of a dysfunctional relational system.
  • True forgiveness only happens with reestablished trust.
  • If you accept the apology, ask what will change moving forward.

You are called into your senior leader's office and asked to sit down. You noticed he seemed preoccupied and a bit sorry. Considering all the history of workplace chaos, your immediate thought was that you were going to be fired.

But instead of delivering the sad news, he said something you did not expect to hear—a sincere, honest apology. "Last week I cut you off during the meeting and excluded you from participating in the discussion and decision-making, which is your proper role for your project; I have realized that I acted wrongly. I must have made you feel terrible. I am very sorry.”

He immediately validated your feelings, and you gladly accepted the apology, leaving the conversation feeling relieved and validated. For the first time, you felt like "finally they see my professional role for what it is."

But that conversation is exactly where the psychological trap may begin. Many, without realizing it, mistake emotional relief for change.

Apologies Don't Mean They Will Not Do It Again

Consider a high-achieving professional, let’s call her Mary, who spends months dealing with a dysfunctional workplace system. For example, she was hired for one thing—to lead a project—then excluded and told what to do instead by an unclear authority figure. Eventually, her boss acknowledged the chaos of what happened, which produced genuine psychological relief, and maybe even forgiveness.

Fourie, Hortensius, and Decety (2020), writing in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, describe forgiveness as involving three interacting psychological processes: cognitive control, perspective-taking, and social valuation. Together, these processes can help a person to be receptive to the other person’s perspective and reassess the relationship. You may accept an apology but decide not to continue the engagement, or you may accept the apology and forgive, giving the relationship a second chance. Ricciardi and colleagues (2013), in their fMRI study, asked participants to imagine or recall hurtful interpersonal situations and instructed them to either forgive or hold a grudge. The fMRI data showed that forgiveness enabled the brain to use logic to calm anger. Holding grudges activated pathways of pain and anger. This tells us that forgiveness is partly an internal process; that is, if you see structural change without an apology, if a person reflects and adjusts their behavior, there may be reconciliation—resolving anger and resentment even when no formal apology was spoken.

When Relief Reduces the Pressure to Change

When our head hurts, and we take Tylenol, the symptoms may go away. When Mary was delivered an apology, it seemed similarly to relieve the symptoms of workplace dysfunction. An apology is a symptomatic solution that provides faster relief than the more difficult fundamental solution, like addressing your headache with a doctor who examines your body and psychological system to fix the root cause. Because an apology brings immediate symptom relief, attention and pressure can shift away from addressing the underlying cause.

An apology can sometimes play the role of a tension reliever. The employee may feel recognized, and the leader may feel that professional relationship issues have been addressed; this makes work-surrounded conflict feel less urgent. The problem arises when the clear air from an apology is mistaken for evidence that the issues have been solved, which can be a trap for conflict avoiders—as the same apology may be redelivered, undermining the moral value of apology and its force.

For example, if you were excluded, and then apologized to for it without moving forward with inclusion, that is not a repair. Repair may need to be matched to the problem's structure. This creates a particularly confusing condition: high recognition, low agency. This distinction may be especially important for high-achieving professionals. They can be highly valued, praised, and relied upon, yet have little influence over the processes that shape the work.

Accept the Apology but Ask What Will Change Moving Forward

When someone delivers a sincere apology, you may choose to accept it as your professional courtesy. It is morally valuable when others recognize what was wrong, but that does not mean you must forgive. For true forgiveness, you need to see what will change moving forward and see them follow through. The goal is not to reject the apology or minimize its value; it is to ensure an apology isn't treated as a substitute for fixing mistreatment.

When accepting an apology, look for a commitment to structural change rather than simply moving on. You may choose to ask, “Now that we agree on what went wrong, what structural changes can we make to avoid repeating the same mistakes?”

item.title: The Return of Extreme Thinness
item.description:
Eating Disorders

The Return of Extreme Thinness

When concern is not the same as body-shaming.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Cultural shifts toward extreme thinness can increase body dissatisfaction and eating disorder risk.
  • Concern about visible changes is not the same as shaming or diagnosing someone.
  • Eating disorders occur across the weight spectrum and cannot be identified by appearance alone.

As a psychotherapist specializing in eating disorders and body image concerns, I have been hearing the same question in different forms lately: How do we talk about the return of extreme thinness without body-shaming women or making assumptions about someone’s health? Patients, family members, and colleagues are noticing that extremely thin bodies seem to be showing up more often in celebrity culture, fashion, advertising, and social media, and they are unsure what to make of it or how to talk about what they are seeing.

These questions often overlap. The renewed appeal of extreme thinness affects how people think about bodies in general, while concern about someone we know comes with much more context than a photograph or video can provide. In both situations, what we see may raise questions, but it is only part of the picture.

Eating disorders affect people of all genders, and body image distress is not limited to women. I am focusing here on women because much of the current conversation about the return of extreme thinness has centered on female celebrities, models, and influencers, and women’s bodies continue to receive an enormous amount of public scrutiny.

When Extreme Thinness Starts Looking Normal Again

Beauty standards are reinforced by what we see again and again. When very thin bodies are the ones being photographed, praised, dressed by designers, and held up as desirable, thinness can become linked with attractiveness, control, success, or acceptance. For someone vulnerable to an eating disorder, restriction may look less alarming and compulsive exercise more like discipline. The contrast feels especially noticeable now because there has been somewhat greater visibility of body diversity in mainstream media in recent years.

I see this rationalization often in my outpatient practice. Someone may say she is trying to be healthier, eat more cleanly, get toned, or take better care of herself while she is also eating less, eliminating more foods, avoiding meals with other people, or spending increasing amounts of time thinking about exercise and her body. None of those phrases sounds especially alarming because they are so familiar in our culture, but the behavior underneath them can tell a different story.

Seeing a thin celebrity does not cause an eating disorder. Eating disorders are far more complex than that, but when thinness is highly rewarded, it can become easier to defend or minimize behaviors that are becoming rigid, compulsive, or harmful.

Eating Disorders Do Not Have a Look

Whenever extreme thinness and eating disorders are discussed together, there is a risk of reinforcing the old idea that an eating disorder is something we should be able to recognize by looking at a person. We cannot, and people can have serious eating disorders in bodies of every size. Someone does not have to appear emaciated to be medically compromised or deeply affected by an eating disorder.

People in larger bodies are especially likely to have restriction or significant weight loss praised rather than questioned. A person may be eating far too little, losing weight rapidly, exercising compulsively, and becoming increasingly preoccupied with food while being congratulated for looking “healthy.” If people are waiting for someone to fit a stereotypical picture of an eating disorder before becoming concerned, many people will be missed.

When I assess someone for an eating disorder, body size tells me very little on its own. I want to know what has changed around food. Are meals being skipped? Have foods or entire food groups disappeared? Has eating become more rigid? Is the person avoiding restaurants or meals with other people?

I ask about exercise, body checking, guilt after eating, anxiety around food, and how much time is being spent thinking about food and weight. I also want to know what else has changed. Family and friends may notice that the person is more tired and irritable, has trouble concentrating, is pulling away from people, is sleeping differently, or is no longer interested in things she usually enjoys. Any one of those changes could have many explanations, but what gets my attention is when several of them are showing up together.

When Concern Is About More Than Appearance

If someone you know has lost a significant amount of weight, you may notice it, and pretending you have not seen the change is not necessarily more respectful than acknowledging it. With a friend or family member, we may also know much more than what their body looks like.

We may notice that she has stopped eating with others, become more rigid about food, changed the way she exercises, withdrawn socially, or seemed exhausted or increasingly anxious. Significant weight loss may be one part of a much larger change, and it can also be concerning in its own right.

I would be careful not to take those observations and turn them into a diagnosis. Saying, “You look anorexic,” “You need to eat a sandwich,” or “Look at how skinny you are” is very different from privately saying, “I’ve noticed you’ve lost a lot of weight, you seem exhausted, and you haven’t been eating with us as much. I’m worried about you.” The second statement does not claim to know what is causing the changes. It tells the person what has been noticed and why there is concern.

With a celebrity, we are usually working from photographs, videos, and whatever pieces of her life are public. We may notice that someone looks very different, but we do not know her medical history, how she eats, whether she has an eating disorder, or what else may explain the change. We can leave those questions alone and still talk about why extremely thin bodies are becoming more visible and desirable again.

Why “You Look Too Thin” Can Be Complicated

Source: David Underland/Unsplash

Some of my patients have told me that hearing they looked “too thin” actually felt reassuring to the eating disorder. The person saying it may have been scared, but the patient heard something very different: the weight loss was visible, and in the eating disorder’s logic, that could feel like success. I keep that in mind when helping families think about what to say.

I would not tell them to pretend they have not noticed significant weight loss or other physical changes, but I would encourage them not to make body size the focus of the entire conversation. Someone may respond very differently to “You’re too thin” than to hearing that her family has noticed she seems exhausted, is avoiding meals, no longer wants to go out with friends, and appears increasingly anxious around food.

Physical changes can still be included. There is nothing inherently wrong with acknowledging that someone has lost a substantial amount of weight when that is genuinely part of what has raised concern, but I would place it alongside the other changes rather than making it the sole focus.

Eating disorders can also affect insight and judgment, especially as someone becomes more entrenched in the illness or more undernourished. A loved one may be trying to communicate fear, while the person with the eating disorder hears proof that the weight loss is noticeable or that she has achieved something. That helps explain why a comment meant as concern may be taken in almost the opposite way.

If You Are Worried About Someone

When someone asks me how to approach a friend or family member, I usually encourage a private conversation that stays close to what has actually been observed. I am less interested in persuading the person that she has an eating disorder than in making sure she knows that people who care about her have noticed changes and are concerned.

That might sound like, “You haven’t seemed like yourself lately. You seem much more anxious around food, you aren’t joining us for meals as often, and I’ve noticed some physical changes too. I care about you, and I’m worried.” It gives the person something concrete to respond to without telling her what her diagnosis is or what her body should look like.

The conversation may not go well. Someone with an eating disorder may become defensive, minimize what is happening, feel embarrassed or angry, or genuinely not recognize how much things have changed.

I would not take that reaction as proof that the concern was misplaced. I would stay away from jokes, sarcasm, arguments about how much someone should weigh, or comparisons to how she looked before. “Just eat,” “You look awful,” and “You don’t look like you have an eating disorder” are not likely to help. Praising weight loss while expressing alarm about the behaviors that may be producing it can also send a confusing message.

We are still remarkably quick to treat weight loss as an accomplishment. The person may enjoy the compliments, but that does not make them harmless. Praise can reinforce the idea that a smaller body is better and create pressure to keep the weight off or continue losing. If some of the weight is later regained, the person may feel as though they have failed or lost something other people valued. For someone vulnerable to an eating disorder, that kind of positive reinforcement can make restriction and other weight-control behaviors harder to recognize as a problem.

Looking at the Whole Picture

The return of extreme thinness is worth talking about without speculating about whether a particular celebrity has an eating disorder. My concern is the way a much thinner body is again being presented as desirable and how that can reinforce eating disorder symptoms.

With someone we know, significant weight loss can be concerning in its own right, especially when it occurs alongside changes in eating, exercise, mood, energy, or behavior. An eating disorder may be a very real possibility, even though appearance alone cannot tell us the diagnosis. We don’t have to dismiss what we are seeing to avoid body-shaming someone, and we don’t have to claim certainty about what is causing it to be concerned.

item.title: Finding Calm at the Water's Edge
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Finding Calm at the Water's Edge

Personal Perspective: Sometimes even adults need a timeout.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • When you find a place that restores and refreshes you, be sure to go back there often.
  • We reset our clocks, computers, and phones. Why not do the same for ourselves?
  • If we don’t take care of ourselves, how can we take care of anybody or anything else?
Over the dunes and on to the shore.
Source: Anton Sharov/Unsplash

If I wore a mood ring, today it would be blue. Dark and murky blue. That blue the sky gets just before a storm. The color of a Monday that dawned too early with too much on my mind and too much on my plate.

Every once in a while, I feel this way. Chalk it up to one of the astrological hazards of Sagittarian life. It happens whenever the archer in me aims so high that the distance between where I am and where I want to be seems unattainable. At times like this I know that, at least for me, there’s only one cure.

As always, I tell myself I don’t have time for this. Got to get to work. Got to get going. And yet, myself tells me I don’t have any choice. Before I change my mind, I hop in the car and get it started, hoping it will do the same for me.

Winding down the road, I hit the brakes as I come up behind an old Oldsmobile. At this pace, I will be lucky to make it to the next traffic light before sunset. As for the pickup truck behind me, it’s clear the driver will soon be taking inventory of my trunk. If the idea here, I tell myself, is to release some stress, here’s a clue. This is not working. And worse, I should be.

First stop: coffee.

Predictably, there’s a line snaking out the door of the cafe. “This place sucks,” grouses the guy in front of me. His friend tells him to calm down. Be patient. Relax. What the world needs now is a little peace. A little serenity. What I need now is a cup of coffee. Maybe a shot of espresso. Or two.

A few more miles and I’m there. For a moment, I just sit in my car. Take a deep breath. Take a sip of coffee. Take a look around. Then, I pull off my sneakers and I’m gone.

Coffee cup in hand, I jump over the stone wall and land on the other side. My brain knows I should be back in my office. But my bare feet, well, they’ve already hit the sand, you see. And once that happens, no force on earth can stop them.

For as long as I can remember, this has been my special place. As close to heaven as I imagine one can get. Why I feel this way is as much a mystery to me as the enigmatic spell that comes over me whenever I’m here.

As I walk hugging the shoreline, some part of me remembers precisely the spot where my dad first taught me how to catch a wave. Waiting for just the right moment, he showed me how to crawl inside the curl, then fly and scream and laugh until I washed up, belly on the sand, boogie board God knows where. Out and in. Out and in. And so it would go until dusk when my parents eventually dragged me home and tucked me in bed where, if I closed my eyes, I could still hear the waves booming. I could still feel the ocean rocking. Rocking me to sleep.

When I was in high school, this is the place where I’d go on my bike after waitressing all day at Howard Johnson’s. To rinse away the day. The greasy residue from serving too many fried clams. To drift away in the afternoon sun, dreaming of nothing in particular. Long before anyone knew about SPFs or holes in the ozone.

It was on this very shore where my friend Andrea and I would run during our trips home from college. “Keep going until you get to the rock,” she coached. No matter how tired we were, no matter how far we ran, we never stopped until the large, gray mass of granite looming on the horizon was beneath our feet.

I came here in a storm once, did I mention that? Nine months and nine days pregnant. “When will this baby ever come?” I shouted to the waves. They just rolled away. But I did get an answer. The very next morning.

And so here I have come once more. To where land meets sea meets sky. Where the earth is ruled by the moon. It’s the same beach. I know that. And yet it’s different now. As am I. I come here for different reasons. Sometimes to remember. Sometimes to forget.

The wet nose of a yellow Labrador nuzzles up against my leg. His teeth are clenched around a tennis ball, dripping with seaweed. I throw the soggy thing as far into the sea as I can. He does what dogs do. He swims after it.

Heading down the beach now are two women. One with a baby in a pack on her back. The other with a baby in a pack on her chest. In their hands, each woman holds a cup of coffee. Clearly, I’m not in this alone.

When I reach the concession stand, I turn and head back. Back toward the rock. The wind is behind me. I’ll make it, of course. I always do.

item.title: August Theory and Midlife Anxiety
item.description:
Midlife

August Theory and Midlife Anxiety

Consider the transition stress that social media calls "August Theory."

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Seasonal transitions can prompt reflection and emotional audits.
  • Midlife transitions can make August feel especially significant.
  • Use August for reflection, not as a deadline for major decisions.

Have you ever experienced Sunday night anxiety? You can't relax and focus on the last bits of the weekend. Instead, you start preparing for the week ahead and get consumed by everything you have waiting for you. We experience August in the same way. If June is Friday night and July is Saturday, August is Sunday afternoon. It is the moment we realize Monday morning is coming, and we start asking ourselves if we are ready for the week ahead. The anxiety we feel isn't necessarily about Sunday or August. It is the anticipation of what is coming next. We shift from the Saturday/July enjoyment of living in the moment to anticipating what is coming next. Instead of enjoying what remains of the weekend or summer, we mentally rehearse responsibilities, decisions, and changes that haven't happened yet.

The August Theory has become a viral trend on social media. It doesn't represent a psychological theory in the scientific sense. But its popularity allows us to reflect on the power transitions have as cues for self-reflection. A change in season, or a birthday, anniversary, new year, or other marker in time can cause us to take stock of where we are and where we're going. TikTok calls August Theory a romantic deadline—the make-or-break month for relationships, dating, and personal goals before the summer ends. However, the theory goes beyond dating. Whether you're 22 or 52, August strips away the lull of summer and forces you to face life/work decisions before the end of Labor Day weekend.

Gen Z's viral trend hits home for those of us on The Right Side of 40 because August is a temporal landmark—a point in time that divides our lives into psychological chapters. It's the "before and after" or the "then and now." In August, we simultaneously hold onto summer and anticipate the structure of fall. The August Theory works because it names a universal human truth—that seasonal thresholds may prompt an emotional audit. Midlifers feel this transition anxiety regarding careers, empty-nesting, and long-term partnerships.

In midlife, that emotional audit can carry additional weight. At 22, September may mean returning to school, defining a new relationship, or starting a career. In midlife, the questions may be different: Am I satisfied with my career? What will life look like after my children leave home? Is this relationship still right for me? What do I want the next decade to look like? The season changes for everyone, but the developmental questions change with us.

We need this emotional audit so we can plan and get ourselves ready for the next stage. It can help midlifers set intentionality. Look beneath some of the most popular versions of August Theory, and you'll see the concerns aren't exclusively for 20-somethings. Circumstances may change, but the psychology remains the same.

Examining August Theory Through a Midlife Lens

1. The situationship reality check:

  • According to social media: This is the time to define the relationship before Labor Day or let it fade.
  • Midlife version: It is time to take stock of undefined relationships or lingering personal projects.

2. The ex resurfacing:

  • According to social media: Exes reach out in August seeking familiar comfort before the fall season kicks into its new routine.
  • Midlife version: Transitions can increase the appeal of familiarity, perhaps in the form of past relationship partners, because it feels safer when the future feels uncertain.

3. Pre-cuffing season panic:

  • According to social media: Lock down a partner so you aren't alone for the winter holidays
  • Midlife version: We fear the "corduroy season," dreading the autumn and winter isolation, less daylight, and rigid routines.

The anxiety of losing summer autonomy hits all generations as we are all triggered by transition stress no matter our age. August may make us feel as though something needs to be decided before Labor Day, but that isn't the same as an actual deadline. You don't have to resolve your relationship, career, empty-nest plan, or next chapter before summer ends. Instead, August can be used as a prompt to be intentional about your decisions.

Practical Strategies for Navigating the August Theory

  1. Distinguish between genuine emotional alignment and fear of entering a new season.
  2. Set intentional boundaries before September schedules overwhelm your calendar. (There is still time.)
  3. Keep some of your summer habits such as outdoor activities, leisure reading, and unstructured time.
  4. Practice micro-transitions. Block out unassigned time in your September calendar to prevent post-Labor Day schedule shock.

You can reclaim August as month of personal clarity instead of the deadline that comes with the death of summer. It can then become the runway from which your next most intentional chapter begins.

item.title: Parallel Parenting vs. Co-Parenting
item.description:
Parenting

Parallel Parenting vs. Co-Parenting

When sharing information with your child's other parent is no longer a choice.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • If info helps your co-parent support your child, it's worth sharing—even when parallel parenting.
  • Sharing info isn't access to your life; it's helping your child feel supported in both homes.
  • Kids carry emotions between homes; parents need context to comfort and guide them effectively.

Q: My co-parent and I have been parallel parenting since our breakup. We communicate as little as possible because keeping our lives separate prevents arguments. Recently, our son came home from his father's house very upset. His grandfather lives with Dad, and they are extremely close. Grandpa has cancer and has become very thin. Our son noticed and was frightened, but he was afraid to ask Dad or Grandpa what was happening. When he came back to my house, he asked if Grandpa was going to die. I didn't even know Grandpa was sick. I was completely unprepared to help him. How do you know when it's time to share information?

A: After a breakup, parents may choose a parallel parenting approach to limit communication and reduce conflict. But parallel parenting doesn't eliminate the need to share information about your child.

The big question is: When does sharing information really become necessary?

A good guideline is this: Your child goes back and forth. At times, the information necessary to support your child may have to go back and forth, too. If knowing something will help your co-parent understand, care for, or support your child, it's probably information worth sharing.

Your son's grandfather's illness is a perfect example.

Balancing Privacy and Your Child's Needs

Grandpa's medical information is private. Dad doesn't have to tell you the details of his father's diagnosis or treatment. But your son is watching someone he loves become very thin. He knows something is wrong. He's frightened. And then he comes to your home carrying that fear.

At that point, Grandpa's illness is no longer information that affects only Dad's household. It’s affecting your child. Now the approach changes.

This is an opportunity for the two of you to decide together how you will support your son. And, it's best if you have discussions like this before the fact.

What does he know?

What has he noticed?

What is he afraid of?

What language are you both using to explain Grandpa's illness?

If Grandpa is dying, what does your son need to understand?

How will you both answer his questions?

You don't have to have identical conversations. But a child facing the possible death of someone he loves benefits enormously when the adults caring for him aren't operating with completely different information.

Too often, estranged co-parents think sharing information means giving an ex access to their personal life.

It doesn't.

Even one conversation between you and Dad changes what happens when your son comes home. Instead of being caught by surprise, you're prepared. You can reinforce what Dad has already explained and offer comfort to your son as he navigates something very painful.

Everyday Examples of Important Information to Share

No matter how estranged you feel, there will be other times when sharing information makes it easier for both of you to support your child. For example:

Your child has a terrible argument with a best friend and is devastated.

Your child gets cut from the soccer team.

A beloved pet dies.

A teacher expresses concern about falling grades.

A close family member is hospitalized.

Your teenager goes through a painful breakup.

A grandparent receives a serious diagnosis.

None of these things necessarily requires a lengthy co-parenting conference. Sometimes a simple heads-up is enough:

“She had a rough day today. Her best friend told her she doesn't want to be friends anymore. She may be pretty quiet tonight.”

Think about your child moving between two homes.

He doesn't stop feeling something because it's transition day.

He doesn't leave his fear at Dad's house when he goes to Mom's.

He doesn't leave his disappointment at Mom's when he goes to Dad's.

Children carry their experiences with them.

When co-parents communicate easily, they often share this kind of information naturally. When they barely speak, they may share only what is specifically required: pickup times, school schedules, medical appointments.

Everything else stays behind an invisible wall.

The problem is that the child walks straight through that wall.

That's what your son did. He left Dad's house frightened about Grandpa and arrived at your house with exactly the same fear. The information didn't make the transition with him, so you had no context for what he was carrying.

There's another important part of this.

Sometimes sharing information does more than prepare the other parent to support the child. It gives that parent context for what the co-parent may be experiencing as well.

Dad's father has cancer.

Dad may be frightened. He may be grieving before his father has even died. He may be exhausted from caregiving while trying to parent his son. His patience may be shorter. His routine may change.

Mom doesn't have to become Dad's emotional caretaker. But knowing what Dad is going through gives her context. There may be a time when Dad asks to change a weekend because his father has a treatment. Knowing what's going on allows Mom to respond to those situations with an understanding she couldn't have if she had no information at all.

And that's an important distinction. Supporting your child's other parent does not mean stepping back into your former relationship. It means recognizing that what happens to one parent can sometimes affect your child and, therefore, changes must be made to match the occasion,

This is why I encourage co-parents to think carefully about information sharing.

Key Questions to Decide What to Share

You don't have to be friends.

You don't have to discuss your private lives.

You don't even have to particularly like each other.

But you do have to recognize that you're parenting the same child.

So, before deciding whether to share something, ask yourself:

"Will knowing this help my child's other parent understand, care for, or support our child?"

If the answer is yes, that's probably information worth sharing.

Remember, whether you're parallel parenting or co-parenting, sharing information isn't about giving your ex access to your life. Sharing information is about giving your children the love and support they need to comfortably live in both homes. Now you are truly "putting the children first."

item.title: Want Your Espoused Values to Matter? It’s Time to CARE
item.description:
Leadership

Want Your Espoused Values to Matter? It’s Time to CARE

We propose the "CARE" framework for leaders to better implement espoused values.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Millennials and Gen Z employees report a gap between desired and lived organizational values.
  • Values are most effective when they guide relationships, performance, and positive change.
  • Leading companies embed values through stewardship, communication, rewards, and accountability.
  • Leaders reinforce values by modeling them consistently and integrating them into daily decisions.

Co-authored by Peter G. Dominick, Dimitra Iordanoglou, and Gregory Prastacos

Strong organizational values can be powerful tools for driving organizations’ success and are also crucial in attracting, retaining, and motivating talent. However, many organizations describe their core values, yet fall short in effectively integrating them into their daily operations.

Three of us (Peter G. Dominick, Dimitra Iordanoglou, and Gregory Prastacos) recently conducted a survey that sheds further light on this. It included almost 1100 Millennials and Generation Z employees from diverse backgrounds, covering a variety of industries. This demographic represents around 45% of the U.S. and global workforces, and is only growing. We found that they desired organizational values that the “Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For” embrace, namely values guiding relationships, desired performance, and positive change. However, our results suggested that these same employees felt their companies were not sufficiently guided by these desired values.

The findings are alarming. They indicate that even though most companies report espouse values that employees desire, many fail to demonstrate, communicate and support them effectively. Such gaps can have detrimental effects on employees’ commitment and performance, and may partially explain the low engagement levels (e.g. “quiet quitting”) and low retention rates among Millennials and Generation Z employees.

So, how can organizations better implement their espoused values? Building on that earlier research, published in the Journal of Business Ethics, which examined the espoused values of the Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For and the practices they use to embed those values into organizational life, we collected, through in-depth interviews, insights from senior managers at nine companies that have been consistently on the list of Fortune's "100 Best Companies to Work For."

We found that the values at these companies intuitively coalesce around the three dimensions celebrated in models of leader effectiveness: people (relationships); results (performance); and continuous learning and innovation (change). In this sense, they implicitly understand values as a form of leadership. Indeed, leaders at these companies are intentional about leveraging values to guide others, influence outcomes, and stay accountable. Their actions converged around four implementation themes. We describe them here as the “Values-CARE” leadership role framework.

C: Values Caretaker

Values caretaking is about stewardship and ensuring the long term-sustainability of an organization’s values. It begins with respecting, even cherishing, the role that values play in shaping the organization’s identity. As one person stressed, “Our values are decades old, so old they are chiseled in stone.” Another noted, “It is ingrained in us to ask how our decisions reinforce our values and culture.”

The caretaker role further includes supporting and institutionalizing values. Several of the organizations we spoke with described having vice presidents of culture who reported directly to their CEOs in addition to their head of human resources. One person highlighted how the role was created in their company in the aftermath of the financial crisis: “We were facing lots of turnover and also lots of new hires…The Director of Culture role was created to help foster continuity.”

There is a curating aspect, too. To be considered a "Great Place to Work," organizations must compile numerous accounts of how they bring their values to life. The benefit of compiling all this information, one spokesperson explained, “is that it provides employees with models for how to live them.”

At other times, the caretaker role involves revisiting espoused values to reflect on what is required to keep them relevant. As an example, a different person pointed out that while diversity has been a long-standing value, their understanding of it has broadened. They recognized how diversity is much more complex (e.g., intersectionality) than when they first started talking about it and shifted their focus more towards inclusion. At other times, revitalizing includes candid self-critiques. “We are not always successful at living up to our values,” one person acknowledged, “but we are committed to them.”

A: Values Ambassador

The ambassador role is about the ways leaders prioritize values-based communication within and outside of their organizations. It includes being the chief spokesperson and role model for the organization’s values. One individual described how every company meeting begins with a five-minute discussion of mission and values. He went on to stress that "these discussions are even more detailed at senior leadership meetings.” Another stressed, “having a CEO who regularly talks about the company’s values has been essential to reinforcing their importance.”

This ambassadorial work permeates interactions at all levels of the companies we spoke with. Almost all expressed some version of this sentiment conveyed to us by one individual: “New associates hear about values from Day 1 as part of orientation and almost every day afterwards.” One organization told us that they regularly fly new hires to the corporate headquarters to meet with the CEO and that they engage new hires in real-time discussions about what represents effective expression of the company values and what does not.

The ambassador role is also about devising better ways to communicate existing values. One person described how they spent several years refining the words they use to define their values. She explained, “Our goal was to make them concise enough so that people would be able to talk about them/recall them.”

R: Values Rewarder

The people we spoke with also stressed how values play an important role in rewarding people. One noted, “Most firms have an 'eat what you kill' approach to senior partner compensation. (We) reward people for sharing work.” Another interviewee stressed employees expect qualified current personnel who embody company values to be given full consideration for advancement, especially to senior positions.

All highlighted how values were built into the performance management process. Several also described annual awards programs to recognize people who represented the best examples of their values in action. One organization noted how this included an award for community service. Another highlighted their everyday values appreciation and recognition system.

E: Values Enforcer

Consider values enforcing to be all the ways in which leaders hold people accountable for living up to their company’s values. This especially includes sanctioning those who violate them in significant ways. “There is zero tolerance for violation of core values,” one person told us. He described two consecutive weeks when senior officers were dismissed by the CEO for not adhering to the company’s values. For their CEO, these dismissal decisions were difficult but clearcut.

Every spokesperson emphasized that values alignment is a key part of their new hire selection process. “We call it being guardians of the culture,” one explained. The spokesperson for another company described how they watch out for people who say “I” too much and are mindful of how interviewees treat receptionists, to enforce values related to collaboration and teamwork.

Values enforcing also includes holding service providers accountable. One person recounted how an external vendor offered them options that, while legal, contradicted their values. Their leader quickly terminated the vendor’s briefing.

Do You CARE?

In too many organizations, espoused values can be platitudes or even sources of cynicism. It’s clear, however, from our survey that espoused values can and should be prized tools for leaders. The companies we spoke to succeed at putting their values into practice because they CARE about them. As Aristotle astutely noted, “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence then is not an act, but a habit.” We think the CARE framework can help organizations ensure that their espoused values are the habits that make them excellent.

Peter G. Dominick is an Industry Professor, and Gregory Prastacos is a Professor, in the School of Business at Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ. Dimitra Iordanoglou is an Associate Professor at Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences, Athens, Greece

item.title: Toward a Better Environment for Our Brains
item.description:
Genetics

Toward a Better Environment for Our Brains

Rethinking the health equation of Gene + Environment.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Large datasets are revealing how our physical environment may influence health.
  • Creating greener, healthier environments may benefit both brain and overall health.
  • Not all environmental risks are modifiable, but some may be changed individually or collectively.
  • Increasing tree canopy, for example, has been associated with lower mortality over time.

I wrote about why nature may be good for our brains in my last post, and just this week, I came across another interesting study that made me think about the question more broadly: How much does the physical environment affect our health and brain?

Impressively, this study was led by medical student. The research team combined high resolution tree canopy estimates, temperature, and mortality data in Chicago over a 10-year period (2011 to 2021). The novelty of this study was not just examining the relationship between tree canopy and health but how changes in tree canopy from year to year were associated with changes in mortality over time.

The finding was striking. Each year-to year-percent increase in tree canopy was associated with about a 10% reduction in mortality. The associations were seen in deaths related to cardiovascular, mental health, musculoskeletal, and respiratory conditions. A 10% reduction in mortality is a whopping number, if we think about what we hope to achieve, say, in a drug trial.

Correlation Is Not Causation

Of course, one of the first lessons in science is that correlation is not causation.

In their study, Chicago’s South and West side had higher temperatures and greater absolute canopy loss over time (despite higher baseline canopy levels) and was associated with increased mortality. These are areas known for economic disadvantage, so we are faced with classic chicken-or-egg dilemma. Was the decline in canopy a reflection of decline in socioeconomic state of the neighborhood? Or perhaps tree canopy was a proxy for other health-promoting factors, such as places to exercise and cleaner air.

This study cannot fully answer what caused what. But it illustrates something else that I find fascinating: epidemiology is changing. Increasingly, researchers can combine large-scale health datasets with detailed information about the physical environments in which people live.

And that is beginning to change how we study neurological disease as well.

Address Can Become Environmental Data

“This is why I don’t have a nice house by the golf course. Not that I cannot afford it.”

That became something of an inside joke last year among us after a study reported an association between living near a golf course and Parkinson's disease.

It has long been known that pesticide exposure maybe one of the risk factors for Parkinson’s disease. Early environmental studies used methods like case-control study, where researchers asked people with and without a disease about where they lived, what jobs they had held, what their diets are and what chemicals or pesticides they remember encountering. These studies taught us a lot, but it is subjective and cannot escape recall bias. I know this firsthand because I have been involved in these types of research.

Instead, recent epidemiological studies using geospatial residential data offer more objective and granular population data. Researchers can map where people lived and overlay those locations with information about agricultural land, golf courses, groundwater, air pollution, traffic, industrial exposures, and other characteristics of the environment.

In the golf-course study, living within one mile of a golf course was associated with 126% higher odds of having Parkinson's disease compared with living more than six miles away. The researchers also examined groundwater vulnerability, and their findings suggested that pesticides reaching groundwater could be one possible explanation.

That does not mean that living near a golf course causes Parkinson's disease. But the geographic pattern raises questions worth investigating.

Another large U.S. study found that greater cropland density within five miles of a residence was associated with Parkinson's disease in parts of the northern Great Plains. Again, agricultural pesticide exposure is one possible explanation.

The Air Around Us

Another rapidly developing area of research examines air pollution.

I had to learn a new term: PM2.5, a fine particulate matter with a diameter ≤2.5 μm that may arise from traffic, combustion, wildfire smoke, industrial activity, An association between areas with higher density of PM2.5 and higher incidence of Parkinson’s is documented. This association has been even more robust with dementia, especially in Alzheimer’s.

I don't mean to be alarmist about these findings. These are statistical differences observed across large populations. They do not tell us whether one particular person will develop Parkinson's disease or dementia. Disease emerges from many interacting factors accumulated over a lifetime.

Disease Risk formula G + E Reexamined

We learn in medical school that health results from complex interaction of G + E, where G is genetic and E is environment.

For neurodegenerative disease, an emerging framework might look something like:

Risk genes + [Place → Chronic Exposures] → Biological Changes → Neurological Vulnerability

It is a complicated framework, but “vulnerability” is not destiny. And because we still do not have cures for many neurodegenerative diseases, anything that might help prevent or delay disease is worth understanding.

So what can we do about it? We cannot change our G. What about E?

Here, we may be able to change a few: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking, and other lifestyle choices come to mind. The focus, traditionally have been working on modifying individual behaviors.

E is of course larger, and includes the air, the water, the temperature, the chemical exposure, the green spaces, and perhaps even the trees growing—or disappearing—around us. And the question we need to re-ask ourselves is this;

"Can some of them be modifiable?" We tended to think the physical environment is fixed and cannot be changed, but we may have some individual agency over the environments we spend time in. For example, taking a walk in the park during our lunch break, spending time in nature, avoiding harsh chemicals when possible, or making our immediate surroundings calming.

Having said that, many environmental conditions are not realistically under individual control.

That is where choices becomes collective. For example, where we plant trees, how we design neighborhoods, how we regulate pollutants, how we protect air and water, are also choices made at the level of communities and societies.

Planting and maintaining trees will not cure Parkinson's disease or dementia. Nor can we conclude from one observational study that planting a tree will make any individual person live longer. But trees provide shade, reduce heat, influence air quality, create spaces for physical activity, and may support psychological and cognitive well-being.

Making our communities greener may offer multiple benefits, and best of all, without much side effect.

Perhaps we need to ask ourselves bigger questions about our modifiable risk factors of health and brain.

What kind of environment do we want to create, for ourselves and for others?

item.title: Design the Familiar, With a Twist
item.description:
Stress

Design the Familiar, With a Twist

Design that evolves at a slow, steady pace is good for how we think and behave.

Posted August 27, 2026

Designing our homes, workplaces, and leisure spaces in ways that consider the passage of time can boost our well-being and our mental and physical health, particularly in these key domains:

1. Lighting

Natural and circadian lighting help your body stay in sync with your location on the Earth, which is a fancy way of saying they'll help you keep track of what time it is and reduce your stress levels, too, all while boosting your mental performance and ability to interact positively with other people. So, open your curtains as wide as the thermal power of your windows permits.

For circadian light without fancy investments, make sure that in each room of your home, there are some warmer white light bulbs and some cooler white ones. Turn on the fixtures with the warmer lights in the morning and evening and use the cooler lights during the middle part of your day.

To even more closely support natural lighting with your electrical lights, it’s great if, during times when you’re using the warmer lights, light levels are, relatively, a little dimmer; cooler lighting, when it’s turned on, should be relatively brighter. Whenever possible, it’s also best to put warmer bulbs in lower lamps, such as those that stand on the floor or are placed on tabletops, and cooler ones higher up, say, in on-ceiling fixtures.

2. Changing Décor

Another way you can mark the passage of time in your home, and to live in a positive, comfortable, biophilic way, is to slightly change your décor every few weeks. Re-arranging/using what you already have is a great way to do so without spending a dime—and rearranging/reusing can do all the same things for you that buying new might.

Trade one air freshener for another or play different sorts of music, for example. Look in the back of your closets, under your bed, and wherever else you might have stashed things; a few of those items can be swapped into more prominent places to change what you see as you look around your home. To keep visual clutter in check, tuck away out of sight one thing currently out on a tabletop, etc., for each one you take out from your closets, etc.

If you change up your home, then, ever so slightly, over time, you’ll have all sorts of clues that will help you keep track of when something happened. Modifying things periodically also adds a new ritual to your life, and rituals also help us note the passage of time. They create a mental latticework that helps you keep track of when things have happened.

Why Design Should Always Incorporate the Familiar

But whatever you do, don’t abandon the familiar.

Predictable is positive (for our minds and often our pocketbooks). We favor the familiar, the understandable in the physical worlds that surround us.

Being around and experiencing familiar things generally makes us comfortable and boosts our mood. We prefer to look at art we find familiar, for example.

Familiar doesn’t mean the same as other things we’ve seen, however. It means that most of the elements in a picture are predictable, but not all of them, for example. If paintings of the British countryside are your thing, for instance, add new art that features rolling hills, etc., but don’t be surprised if you feel like purchasing an image completed with green rolling fields and a few purple cows. Make sure those purple cows find a way into your living room.

A bonus from being in a familiar sort of environment: When the world around us is relatively familiar, odds are we’ll be in a more trusting mood. Familiarity is particularly desirable when we’re stressed, as it helps us feel less tense.

Physical things that are familiar can suggest all sorts of positive memories we associate with times past. But object-associated memories can be a reason to make a change as well. If something really negative happened somewhere—you learned of an unexpected death while sitting in your breakfast nook, for example—changes in the décor may be in order. You might consider changing the upholstery on the seats in that nook. The physical changes won’t eliminate that negative experience, but, ultimately, a design modification can weaken links that bring it quite as forcefully top-of-mind.

Design with time to design good times.

item.title: The Power of Choosing Enough Over Chasing Everything
item.description:
Self-Help

The Power of Choosing Enough Over Chasing Everything

How defining "enough" for this season can help us pursue what matters.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Wanting more isn’t the problem; needing more to feel enough can be.
  • Choosing enough isn’t settling, giving up, or becoming less ambitious.
  • Enough is a decision we get to make for ourselves, for the season we’re in.

Maybe enough and being content with enough isn't where ambition ends. Maybe it's where desperation finally ends.

That's something I wrote in a journal entry this time last year.

At the time, I was noticing this pattern in almost every area of my life, both personally and professionally. I'd accomplish something, and for a moment, it felt like the answer. Then, I'd realize it didn't bring the lasting fulfillment I'd hoped for.

I was thinking about all the ways I was chasing the next thing, and I realized I needed to ask myself: When is enough, enough? And how often are we moving the finish line without even realizing it?

Why More Feels Like the Default

It can feel like there is always more to accomplish, more to earn, more to improve, more to give, and more to become. Part of this is just about how we're wired. We're designed to be in a place where we're adapting, striving, and seeing if there is a better or different way of looking after ourselves. There's also something called hedonic adaptation that psychologists talk about. It happens when we work toward something, we get it, and for a while it feels wonderful. Then it becomes our new normal, and the feeling fades. The job, the relationship, the material thing, or the milestone that was supposed to be the answer to everything turns out to be one good, meaningful thing among many, not a finish line after all. So, we look for the next one.

For me, I've built a career on skills, knowledge, and gifts I care about deeply, and for a long time I believed that if I ever said, "This is enough," I'd be doing a disservice to those gifts, to my family, and to the people I'm here to serve. So I kept going, until I noticed what I was actually doing was staying in a perpetual state of chasing, and that chasing isn't the same thing as growing.

I don't think wanting more is the problem. I think the challenge comes from needing more to feel like we are enough.

Having Enough, Doing Enough, Being Enough

When I started paying closer attention to this tension, I noticed it tends to show up in three different ways.

Having enough: This is about what we actually need. When we operate out of desperation or the belief that "more" will make us safe or complete, we're running from a feeling of scarcity, while when we operate from a place of enough, we're recognizing what we already have and move from a place of abundance instead.

Doing enough: This is about our productivity and contribution. We each have gifts worth sharing with the world, but sharing them should come from a place of abundance and overflow, not from trying to earn our worth by staying depleted. Giving from an empty cup isn't sustainable, and our value isn't determined by how much we check off our to-do lists.

Being enough: This is the deepest layer. Who are we without the accomplishments, the possessions, and the external validation? It can feel hard to grasp the deepest sense of our worth and actually believe it. My invitation here is to think about a newborn. A newborn hasn't achieved anything yet, and no parent loves that baby any less for it. We have value and are enough simply because we exist, without having to earn, win, or prove anything.

What Is Enough for This Season?

Here's a perspective shift: Enough is a decision we get to make for ourselves, for the season we're in.

The reality is, we will never have enough of what we do not need. So the invitation is to pause and get honest about what you actually need, not what the world keeps telling you should be doing, ought to be doing, or could be doing.

This isn't about settling or becoming less ambitious. It's about deciding what enough looks like right now, in this particular season, in some key areas, and giving yourself permission to enjoy what's there before looking for the next thing to chase.

Maybe a season of focusing on family means redefining what enough looks like professionally. Maybe enough at work means doing meaningful work without adding more to your plate right now. Enough for your health might mean choosing practices that actually sustain you, rather than turning your well-being into another optimization project. Maybe enough at home means deciding the kitchen baseboards do not, in fact, need to be cleaned today. Perhaps one area of your life needs more attention right now, while another is allowed to simply be good enough.

This is the work: getting radically clear about what enough means for you when it comes to your work, your relationships, your home, your health, or what you're asking of yourself, and then letting enough be enough.

My gentle invitation is to ask yourself:

  • What does "enough" look like for me in this season of my life?
  • Am I moving toward something I value, or am I trying to outrun the feeling that what I have isn't enough?
  • How can I honour the sense of agency that comes from deciding, "This is enough for me," and truly enjoy it?

There's a very different energy between wanting to do something because it matters to us and feeling like we need to do something so we can finally feel worth, safe, successful, or enough.

Final Thoughts

In a world that is very good at moving the finish line, it's easy to get caught in the relentless pursuit of more. It's the when-then mindset that can keep us striving for "everything" and rob us of our joy and contentment in the present with what we have.

My final invitation is to think about where you are right now in your life. If your 20-year-old self, or even your 5-year-old self, could see this version of you, they would likely be amazed by who you have become, the experiences you've had, the memories you've made, and the connections you've built. There was probably a season where you were working toward or wishing for many of the things you have today.

Choosing enough for this season isn't giving up on what's next. It's giving yourself permission to live inside what you've already built and to savour what's here, right now.

So, maybe enough isn't where ambition ends. Maybe it's where the desperation, the hustling, and the constant proving finally get to rest.

item.title: Why Every Art Collector Should Visit Dataland
item.description:
Creativity

Why Every Art Collector Should Visit Dataland

A new musuem in Los Angeles presents data instead of objects.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Dataland offers a glimpse of the museum of the future.
  • This new museum transforms data into art and makes visitors part of the experience.
  • It challenges traditional ideas about what can be collected, created, and preserved.
DATALAND
Source: AI Generated

My friend David Spoelstra, president of MediaMachine LLC, recently visited Dataland in Los Angeles. What he told me was fascinating and applies to a new area of collecting: data. I wrote about this previously, when Dataland was still a dream. Now, it is a concrete building with exhibits and receiving visitors. Here is an update.

Collectors arriving at Dataland may expect yet another immersive digital experience. They leave having encountered something different. Dataland is a museum where data itself becomes the medium and visitors engage with artwork generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

Refik Anadol and Dataland

How does this happen? Refik Anadol, the museum's creator, uses what he calls “data painting,” but he does not apply paint to canvas. Instead, he loads multiple collections of images and information into an AI system. The result is moving, colorful images that seem like a dream. When projected on a large screen, they become mesmerizing.

For the museum’s inaugural exhibition, Machine Dreams: Rainforest, large scientific datasets incorporating plants, birds, insects, coral reefs, weather patterns, and other natural phenomena were combined to create continuously evolving visual landscapes. Thus, each guest's visit is different; no two are exactly alike.

During the rainforest experience, towering projections surround visitors with swirling orchids, butterflies, moving water, and forests that appear to breathe. Eighty-four projectors create 50 billion pixels of imagery that dissolve and reform in ways no human artist could manually paint. Music shifts continuously, mixing natural sounds with orchestral passages that deepen the emotional effect.

Participant Physiology

Visitors engage with this experience by wearing biometric wristbands that track physiological measures such as heart rate and skin conductivity. David was especially enthusiastic about this feature. Along with observing the artwork, he could see how his body reacted to what he was experiencing.

My recent post, “Why Art Moves Us: Body and Brain,” is relevant here. In it, I described how researchers have demonstrated that viewing physical art, such as a canvas in front of us, can have a physiological effect on our bodies and brains. The same is true of AI-generated art.

The Infinity Room in Dataland surrounds guests with luminous landscapes that apparently stretch beyond the physical walls. This creates uncertainty: One cannot tell where the architecture ends and imagination begins. Another space, the Latent Gallery, displays AI-generated interpretations of nature that vacillate between recognizable forms and abstraction. The Sanctuary brings a visit to its close. This space encourages quiet reflection as digital imagery, sound, and light merge into an unexpectedly meditative experience.

At the end, visitors receive personalized chocolates inspired by the data generated during their experience. (This sounds a bit gimmicky to me; I wonder how physiological recordings could relate to chocolate.)

In Conclusion

Not everyone will embrace Dataland. Some traditional art lovers insist that algorithms cannot replace an artist's hand. Others remain uneasy about artificial intelligence entering creative fields. Still, throughout history, every major artistic innovation—from photography and video art to digital media—has initially been dismissed by some critics.

Dataland is not attempting to replace painting, sculpture, or traditional museums. Instead, it aims to expand our understanding of what art can become when creativity collaborates with computation. It's a new concept for collectors to understand, and it may be our future.
