item.title: The Zen of the Closed Loop
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Zen of the Closed Loop

Process boredom, not cognitive decline, may be the real cost of AI today.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive decline is the wrong worry. The cost is process boredom: hard work with no whole thought to hold.
  • Effectance, the drive to see your own effect on the world, requires a closed loop.
  • The pivot window back into non-AI infused work is still open for a bit—don't wait.
  • For humanity to succeed with AI, we need to get a handle on its process.

In 1997, Ernest Bates bought into a hillside in Napa. He was one of the first three Black board-certified neurosurgeons in the United States, the first Black student to graduate from Johns Hopkins’s undergraduate college, and the founder of a publicly traded medical-equipment company. By 2000, he had stopped practicing and was making cabernet. Friends thought it was a hobby. They were wrong about the category. It was a pivot.

The Current Narrative: Chatbots Are Making Us Stupider

The dominant story about AI and human cognition right now is that chatbots are making us stupider. A recent BBC Future piece marshals MIT researchers Pattie Maes and Nataliya Kosmyna on “cognitive offloading” — the worry that frictionless AI is producing a “stupidogenic” society the way cheap processed food produced an obesogenic one. The evidence is real. The diagnosis is not, I think, the right one. I’ll leave that for another day, but suffice to say that working with AI won’t be easy.

The sharper problem is not that humans are getting cognitively weaker. It is that when machines reason and draft faster and better than the human in front of them, the residual role left for the human collapses to prompting, approving, and pasting. We are retained as quality judges and safety handlers. The thinking is no longer ours to do. It is structurally boring—call it process boredom. The work can stay demanding and still be unfulfilling; difficulty was never where the satisfaction came from. In May, I wrote that boredom was not quite the right word. Process boredom is what was missing.

The mechanism here is old. In 1959, the psychologist Robert White published a paper arguing that humans have an intrinsic motivation he called effectance—the satisfaction of producing a visible effect on the environment and seeing that the effect was, in fact, yours. White’s claim was that this motivation is not reducible to hunger or status, and that it requires a closed loop: the person doing the work has to be the same person who can see whether it succeeded.

Prompting a model that drafts the deck that disappears upstream activates none of this. What breaks is not only the loop but the wholeness of the thought. Judging quality is a fragment: you assess what arrived. Safety handling is another: you catch what must not leave. Neither fragment begins anywhere.

Effectance belongs to the whole arc, from intention to landed effect. The supervisor holds pieces of it, never the whole. And the part of the work that used to feel like effectance—the building, the structuring, the figuring out—now happens one layer of abstraction away, inside the model.

Meanwhile the loaf of bread either rose or it didn’t. The motorcycle hummed again, or not. The cabernet, three years on, either tastes like cabernet, or it doesn’t. The pipe holds pressure, or it doesn’t. These are answerable work: domains where the work answers back to the person who did it, without an intermediary translating the result.

AI’s Impact on the Physical vs. Knowledge Work Divide

A skeptic will say this is just the old physical-versus-knowledge divide, and the divide is collapsing. The skeptic is half right. AI is absorbing the cognitive parts of physical work too: operators on the factory floor now get real-time AI support, and the mechanic spends much of the shift running diagnostics and installing parts where robots cannot yet reach.

But the convergence runs differently on each side. On the physical side, what remains for the human still closes the loop—the car starts, the vine fruits. On the knowledge side, what remains is the prompt, the quality check, and the paste. The asymmetry, not the divide, is what matters.

The benefits of working in domains where the loop closes are not metaphorical. A 2025 systematic review of crafts-based interventions across 19 studies—pottery, woodwork, embroidery, papercraft—found short-term improvements in mood, anxiety, self-efficacy, and life satisfaction. Neither is the toll. NIOSH research finds that construction workers in the United States die from drug overdose and suicide at rates higher than the workforce overall. Vineyard work in August in Napa is hot, repetitive, and it punishes the body. Any honest revaluation has to hold both ends.

If you have been considering this—the workshop, the vineyard, the trade school, the farm—the window is open now. The cognitive premium on knowledge work is compressing fast, and the residual role on the knowledge side is the boring part. The operator side still closes its loop. None of it favors patience.

Acting on it is harder than seeing it.

First, the test is not whether the domain is physical. It is whether the work answers back to you without translation—and whether the thought that produced it was yours throughout. A paragraph judged by a reader is closed-loop. A surgical outcome witnessed by the surgeon is closed-loop. A spreadsheet that disappears into a stakeholder’s slide is not.

Knowledge professionals have a second, harder problem: they tend to import their existing status into new domains, which collapses the apprenticeship that closed-loop work requires. Bates did not arrive in Napa as a famous neurosurgeon making famous-neurosurgeon wine. He arrived as a beginner, with sore hands.

The third is the one I keep returning to. The new domain has to be allowed to produce the lift, and the lift requires that the body show up—repeatedly, at cost. Showing up once a quarter to admire your own vineyard does not close the loop. The loop requires presence, repetition, and the willingness to let small visible competences accumulate against time, comfort, status, and sleep. Working with AI should hurt. Pushing yourself. Challenging the AI. Long nights. Frustration. Failures.

Bates died in March 2024, at 87, still a partner in the winery. The wine went on answering back. The hands hurt the whole way. When did your hands last hurt? And was it for the right reason?

item.title: Did You Grow Up Feeling You Were Not Good Enough?
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Did You Grow Up Feeling You Were Not Good Enough?

New research offers five powerful strategies to recover from narcissistic parenting.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • If you grew up feeling you were not good enough, you may have had narcissistic parenting.
  • The traumatic effects of narcissistic parenting can follow us into adult life.
  • Setting boundaries and limiting contact can help heal from narcissistic family dynamics.
Source: OER Conestoga College (2021)/CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Did you grow up feeling that you were not good enough, constantly seeking approval from the people around you? If this sounds familiar, you may have had a narcissistic parent. Parental behavior can have powerful effects on their children’s lives.

Parents with narcissistic traits are self-centered, lack empathy, and have a strong sense of entitlement. Constantly demanding attention and admiration, they can neglect and emotionally manipulate their children, using guilt, fear, and shame to control them (Ghasemi Rahmatabadi et al., 2026). To maintain dominance, they may lie and use gaslighting to make their children doubt themselves (Burleson & Dutton, 2026).

The traumatic effects of such parenting can follow us into adult life, affecting our mental health, personal identity, and future relationships.

Children of parents with narcissistic traits can grow up with self-doubt, low self-esteem, and feelings of inadequacy. They can experience an internalized negative voice or inner critic that tells them they’re not good enough (Mao et al., 2026; Sokova et al., 2025).

These children, especially daughters, may experience persistent shame, anxiety, and feelings of inferiority (Burleson & Dutton, 2026). Fearing rejection and having difficulty setting healthy boundaries, they may become people-pleasers, striving to gain others’ approval (Burleson & Dutton, 2026; Ghasemi Rahmatabadi et al., 2026).

But if you experienced parental narcissism, you can live a healthier, more balanced life. New research (Burleson & Dutton, 2026) reveals five ways to recover and cope more effectively.

1. Distancing Yourself. You can find relief in solitude and activities that bring you greater peace of mind and happiness. And now that you’re an adult, you can limit exposure to this parent, setting boundaries in communications and on visits.

2. Experiencing Grief Over the Lack of Family Support. Seeing friends with healthy families whose members love and support each other can trigger feelings of loss, reminding you of what you missed in your family of origin. It’s important to mindfully feel your feelings, realize that it’s not your fault, and release uncomfortable feelings.

3. Giving Yourself Self-Compassion. The next step is self-compassion, reparenting yourself with the care, understanding, and emotional support you need. Psychologist Kristin Neff’s three steps to self-compassion involve:

  • Mindfully acknowledging what you’re feeling
  • Realizing that it’s only human to feel this way
  • Treating yourself kindly as you would a dear friend (Neff, 2011; Neff & Miyagawa, 2026)

You can say to yourself, “I feel sad...nervous...worried...lonely” or something else. Then tell yourself that it’s only human to feel this way. And, finally, be kind and caring to yourself, perhaps saying something like, “Sweetheart, I know how you feel, and I’m here for you. We’ll get through this.”

4. Gaining Clarity and Insight. It can help to recognize and document the pattern of narcissistic neglect, writing down what happened and how it made you feel. Psychologist James Pennebaker’s research reveals how writing down our feelings about a negative experience can help us gain insight and heal (Pennebaker, 1997; Pennebaker et al., 2014).

5. Taking Positive Action. When you’ve gained a greater understanding of the effects of narcissistic parenting in your family of origin, you can begin building a healthier, more balanced life. Becoming more aware of your own feelings, you can set healthier boundaries. You can also create a family of choice: a circle of people who love, care, and support each other.

And if you are still struggling with the effects of narcissistic parenting, you can consult a therapist to help you work through it all.

Whatever happened years ago in your family of origin, you are a unique and valuable individual who deserves to live a life of greater peace of mind, loving acceptance, and new possibilities.

This post is for informational purposes and should not substitute for psychotherapy with a qualified professional.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Gargalesis and Knismesis: The Science Behind Tickling
item.description:
Laughter

Gargalesis and Knismesis: The Science Behind Tickling

Why can't we tickle ourselves?

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • It is almost impossible to tickle yourself because touch needs to be unexpected to tickle.
  • Two different types of tickle touch generate either laughter or irritation.
  • A better understanding of tickle perception will help in the development of effective touch therapy.
A classic tickle stimulus and response
Source: David Shankbone, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Are you ticklish? Not everyone is. Children tend to be more ticklish than adults, and factors like mood, thickness of the skin, or physical health can affect how likely you are to find a particular touch enjoyable or just plain annoying (Kilteni, 2025). However, despite the fact that philosophers from Socrates to Aristotle and scientists from Galileo to Darwin have studied ticklishness for centuries, there is still no clear consensus on what it means to be tickled.

The word “tickle” itself probably comes from the Middle English word “tikelen” meaning "touch with repeated light touches in some sensitive part so as to stimulate pleasurably or cause a peculiar and uneasy or thrilling sensation in the nerves" (Harper, n.d.). Notice that there are two kinds of outcomes possible when we are tickled: laughter or discomfort. These two outcomes suggest that not all tickles are the same, and indeed, two kinds of tickle are described in the literature. The tickling we engage in with children or loved ones, where the aim is to produce laughter, is called gargalesis (from the Greek for to tickle) and is one of the earliest triggers for laughter in infants. We use gargalesis to provoke laughter in social bonding with other humans (Kilteni, 2025).

The second kind of tickle, which leads to annoyance or discomfort, is called knismesis (from the Greek for to itch). Gargalesis and knismesis are produced by two distinct types of touch. Knismesis is produced by feather-light touches, on almost any body part (Harris, 2012). Think of the feeling of a bug walking on your arm. That stimulus probably makes you swipe your hand down your arm or shake the limb to dislodge the bug, rather than laugh. It’s irritating, not funny. You can produce knismesis in your own body, or someone else can produce it.

Gargalesis is produced by a somewhat heavier touch, repetitively applied to a specific body location (typically, soles of the feet, underarms, ribs). For most of us, gargalesis occurs only when touch is applied by another person. It is almost impossible to tickle yourself. It is this last characteristic, and the exceptions to it, that have sent investigators looking in the brain.

Touch researchers make a distinction between active and passive touch. According to Gibson (1962), “Active touch refers to what is ordinarily called touching.” When we reach out and grab something to find out what it is, we are using active touch. We’ve planned and initiated the touch. Passive touch, on the other hand, is when someone or something else touches us. Like kids in the car pestering their siblings, eliciting the classic sibling response of “stop touching me!”

The distinction between active and passive touch is important because these two kinds of touches tell us different things about the world. Gibson says active touch could also be called tactile scanning, because we use it to explore in the same way we use our eyes to scan the world around us. Active touch tells us about size, texture, and temperature. Passive touch tells us about a hidden threat or surprise.

Active touch and the efference copy (EC)
Source: Michelle Costanzo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Neurologically, active and passive touch also differ from one another. Active touch involves a command to move the body to touch the world, while passive touch lacks a movement component. This difference, moving vs. being moved, is thought to be at the root of our inability to tickle ourselves.

When you reach out to explore an object in the environment, your motor cortex sends commands to the muscles of your arm and hand, telling them to extend toward the objects you are reaching for. Simultaneously, a second, duplicate copy of those commands is generated, called an efference copy (EC). The EC is a prediction of the sensory consequences of the movement you are making (Latash, 2021). If the prediction matches the incoming feedback, your brain suppresses or even cancels your reaction to the touch.

When you experience passive touch from someone else, there is no movement command generated, no EC sent about what to expect, and no suppression of our response. We are unexpectedly tickled, and we involuntarily laugh. Laughter in this case is a social signal that tells us and the people around us that we’re happy, that we are playing, and there is no threat (there are other kinds of laughter that signal very different emotions, but that’s for another blog).

In a series of experiments, Blakemore, Wolpert, and Frith (2000) manipulated a tickle stimulus delivered to the palm of the hand. The participants either moved their hand in an “S” shape under a stationary stimulus, or that stimulus was moved by the experimenter. The participants rated the ticklishness in several conditions (active and passive movements, and with feedback delayed or rotated so that it didn’t match the prediction the participants would make). Participants rated the movement as more ticklish when it did not match their prediction, even when the movement was self-produced.

They used the same task to examine a group of schizophrenic patients who reported that they did not feel in control of their own behaviors. The schizophrenic group rated the self-produced and externally produced tickles as equally tickly, suggesting a possible abnormality in the system allowing us to distinguish between self-produced and externally produced touch.

Packheiser et al. (2024) note that touch has powerful benefits to physical and mental health “from facilitating growth and development, to buffering against anxiety and stress, over the lifespan of the animal.” Understanding how we distinguish between the touch of others and ourselves can help develop effective touch interventions, like kangaroo care for newborns and massage for adults.

item.title: Today’s Kindergartners Have Never Known a Screen-Free World
item.description:
Parenting

Today’s Kindergartners Have Never Known a Screen-Free World

We need to talk about screen habits long before kindergarten.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Screens too often replace the everyday interactions young children need to learn, connect, and grow.
  • School readiness begins at birth through talking, reading, playing, and responsive interaction.
  • Technology isn’t the enemy; the goal is to keep screens from becoming the default for connection.
  • Pediatric care can help families build reading and interaction into daily life from infancy.

Every fall, a new group of children walks into kindergarten carrying backpacks that look almost as big as they are. This year’s class has something else in common: They’ve never known a world without tablets, smartphones, streaming video, and screens designed to hold their attention.

For parents, conversations about children and screens can quickly become overwhelming. As a pediatrician, I want to be clear about the importance of screen time recommendations during the earliest years. Babies learn best through interaction with the people and world around them. Other than video chatting, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends avoiding routine screen media for children younger than 18 months and keeping screen use limited and intentional as children get older. But there’s another part of this conversation that deserves just as much attention. When a baby or young child is looking at a screen, we also need to think about what they are not doing during that time.

During the first five years of life, children are developing at an extraordinary pace. Long before they enter a classroom or learn to read, their brains are being shaped through interactions with the people around them. They hear the rhythm of language when a parent talks to them in the grocery store. They learn that communication goes back and forth when they babble and someone responds. They begin connecting words with objects when a caregiver points to a picture in a book and names what they see.

These interactions may look ordinary from the outside, but they’re doing important developmental work. That is why the conversation about technology needs to begin much earlier than kindergarten.

What Screens Replace

A young child does not need every waking minute filled with an activity designed to teach them something. Some of the experiences that support healthy development are remarkably simple.

A baby makes a sound and waits for someone to answer. A toddler sits on a parent’s lap and turns the pages of a favorite book, sometimes skipping ahead or going backward. A preschooler gets bored and turns a cardboard box into a house, a spaceship, or a place for stuffed animals to sleep. These moments give children opportunities to listen, respond, imagine, notice, and connect.

Screens can certainly be part of family life, and technology itself isn’t the enemy. The concern is that screens are very good at occupying time that might otherwise contain these small interactions. When a device fills every quiet moment, children have fewer opportunities to initiate conversation, invent their own play, explore their surroundings, or simply see what happens when they are bored.

Parents shouldn't feel guilty for handing a child a tablet while they make dinner, answer an email, or get through a long flight. Parents are managing jobs, households, siblings, and countless other demands. What matters is making sure it does not become the default replacement for interaction. While content matters, even educational apps can crowd out some of the important human touch points that help to shape young brains and relationships.

School Readiness Starts Long Before School

When we talk about preparing children for kindergarten, we often think about what they should know by the first day, like counting, recognizing letters, or writing their name. Such skills matter, but children also arrive at school with years of experiences that have shaped how they communicate, listen, manage frustration, explore ideas, and relate to other people.

For example, a child who has spent years participating in conversations has practiced taking turns before knowing what conversational turn-taking means, and all it required was interaction with a caregiver.

This is one reason pediatric care can play such an important role in early learning. At Reach Out and Read, we begin talking with families about reading and relationships during infancy. During well-child visits, clinicians provide books and guidance that help families make shared reading part of everyday life.

The book matters; studies suggest that print encourages more active engagement and fewer distractions. But while the book matters, so does what happens around it.

Families are going to continue living with technology, and today’s children will need to learn how to use it. Trying to re-create a childhood without screens is neither realistic nor necessary. What we can do is become more intentional about protecting the experiences we know young children need.

That might mean keeping a few books within reach and reading together before bed. It could mean talking with a baby while changing a diaper, asking a toddler what they notice on a walk, or allowing a preschooler to spend a little time figuring out what to do when no entertainment has been provided.

It can also mean putting our own phones down, because children notice where our attention lands, too.

The children entering school this fall have grown up in a world that competes for their attention in ways previous generations did not experience. The next generation will likely encounter even more technology, and at even younger ages.

This all makes the earliest years more important than ever.

item.title: "Life Crafting": Finding Your Life Purpose
item.description:
Self-Help

"Life Crafting": Finding Your Life Purpose

Bring peace and meaning to your life by finding your purpose.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • People are meant to live meaningful lives rather than merely exist.
  • "Life Crafting" is one of many steps we can take to find our life purpose.
  • We can pursue a meaningful life at any age.
Source: LabRobotUIGear/Leonardo.AI

Let’s face it, we all need a reason to get out of bed in the morning. As humans, we aren’t meant to merely trudge through life, living paycheck to paycheck or just accumulating more meaningless stuff. At some point, for many people, a "chasing the carrot" existence is no longer enough. We may yearn for a more meaningful way of life, a passion, or purpose that makes our heart sing, or beat a little stronger. Finding our purpose can provide us with a powerful motivation to rise in the morning with excited anticipation and maybe even joy.

Far too many individuals go through their entire lives without pursuing their true purpose or passion. Finding one’s purpose—a meaningful life—need not be a rarely attained luxury. In fact, living a meaningful life has even been linked to improved health and lowered stress, as well as improved well-being.

Would You Go to Extremes for Your Purpose?

Like most of you, I like a cozy, comfortable life, which I’ve experienced for much of my life—all the usual things we’ve come to expect in a North American lifestyle. Even with a career, though, I came to a point at which I still felt like there was an important key aspect that was missing.

Deep in my soul, I felt there was more that I was supposed to be accomplishing to help people, animals, the planet, or all of the above. That’s when my husband and I packed up our lives and moved abroad.

While at times, making a dramatic change can propel you into journeying into the inner stirrings of your heart, you probably don’t need to make such an extreme change in your life to fulfill your purpose. Your purpose may even be right under your nose.

Zeroing In On Your Heart’s Longings

What does your heart long for? Maybe you’ve been feeling an inner nudge that it’s time for a change, but didn’t know where to start. Perhaps it’s time to sit down with a pen, paper, or laptop and an open mind to dive deeply into your inner yearnings for meaning in your life.

When One Door Closes, Another Opens

Often the true fulfillment for which we’ve been searching occurs when a job ends, or another dramatic life change occurs. This may encourage us to rethink our current situation and consider whether it’s really fulfilling our deepest desires. Or maybe it’s just that dull ache inside that whispers, “I’m meant to do more.” Perhaps this is your soul calling out to you, longing for meaningful activity. Meaningful activity itself is associated with important basic psychological needs, including autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which we all need.

It’s Never Too Late

At 48, my close friend has recently decided to pursue law school to move forward on her dream of becoming an environmental lawyer. While it has long been believed that adult brain function peaks at around age 25, recent studies have exploded that myth. In one study, University of Cambridge researchers found that our personality and cognitive function stabilize or even grow from our early 30s through our late 60s. Through a process called neuroplasticity, neurons can even carve out new pathways to fire in ways that haven’t been used previously, especially if we maintain a healthy lifestyle.

Thus, being a mature, middle-aged, or even senior adult is no reason to forgo one's dream of a meaningful life. In fact, as we accumulate additional life experience, it adds to the richness of our lives and assists us in narrowing down our true heart’s desires. Leading a meaningful life and having social support have also been associated with a higher degree of happiness, including among older adults.

The Soul-Searching Begins: "Life Crafting"

So, if this resonates, find a quiet time and place to search your mind and heart for your soul-stirrings. There’s even a technique called Life Crafting that may help you with the process of finding and pursuing your life purpose. Maybe it’s a secret talent you’ve been hiding or perhaps just a desire to make the world a better place. You are important, and this rapidly changing planet needs you. I’m confident you have your own special gift that you can share with others to help in a meaningful way. What better time than now to pursue your life’s purpose?

I believe in you.

item.title: The 'Bless and Release' Approach in Dating
item.description:
Mating

The 'Bless and Release' Approach in Dating

A new approach emerges as an alternative to ghosting or 'Caspering' in dating.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • A "bless and release" entails firmly saying that you don't feel a romantic match between the two of you.
  • A "bless and release" also includes thanking the other person and wishing him or her the best for the future.
  • It should be clear, eliminate any guesswork, and save both of you a whole lot of time, effort, and energy.
  • A "bless and release" can be part of you taking more charge of your dating life and deciding what you want.
A "bless and release" entails gently but firmly telling the other person that you don't feel a romantic match between the two of you and wishing him or her the best for the future.
Source: Muhammet Raşit Kaplan/Pexels

"Bless and release" may sound like the reverse order of what might happen with a sneeze. But on social media and the Internet, it's being touted as a graceful way to end a particular dating situation so that you can move on to others. Once you know that a person is not a good fit for you, you could use a "bless and release"—gently but firmly telling the other person that you don't feel a romantic match between the two of you and wishing him or her the best for the future.

The "bless and release" is about being clear and concise. There are even sample scripts to do the "bless and release" floating out there, such as, "Thanks for hanging out. But I am not feeling a romantic connection here. Good luck out there." Or "Good chatting with you. However, I don't see us being a match and wish you the best."

Not exactly William Wallace in Braveheart type of stuff. It doesn't involve any over-explaining, dramatic statements, equivocation, negative statements, or anything that might leave a "mess and release" situation instead. The "bless and release" is about setting clear boundaries, making it obvious that you are releasing the other person kind of like you would a fart—in the nicest way possible, though—so that you have room for someone else.

The 'Bless and Release' Is a Clear Alternative to Ghosting or 'Caspering'

The "bless and release" has emerged as a clear alternative to all the ghosting and "Caspering" that people are seeing—or maybe not seeing until after it happens—out there in the dating world. Ghosting and Caspering are when you disappear without any explanation, either abruptly or gradually. These can be very passive and seemingly easy ways to exit stage left, especially for those who are conflict-averse.

However, ghosting and Caspering ain't so easy on everyone involved, including yourself. Not directly telling someone that your potentially romantic interaction is over can leave things vague, with the other person wondering what's going on for a while and you expending energy to maintain pretenses. By contrast, the "bless and release" should eliminate any such guesswork and save both of you a whole lot of time, effort, and energy—time, effort, and energy that could be spent finding and being with a better fit.

The 'Bless and Release' Can Help You Choose What You Want

A "bless and release" can be part of you taking more charge of your dating life. Instead of relying on other people to determine how things proceed, you are doing so. You are the one who decides what does and does not fit you romantically, rather than just waiting to see who chooses you.

This would be a fitting way to proceed because, ultimately, dating is about finding the right mutual fit. The longer you stay with someone who is not the right fit, the less time you have to find and be with someone who is. So, "bless and release" is all about "if it does not fit, you must admit it"—admit it to yourself and the other person, and take action more quickly to clear out your dating space.

Some Cautions About the 'Bless and Release'

Of course, treat the "bless and release" like you would a fart. Once it is out there, you can't pull it back in. If you end up rescinding the "bless and release" at some point in the future, the person will no longer take it seriously. You won't have much credibility if you are like, "Good chatting with you once again. However, as I mentioned two months ago and then two weeks ago, I don't see us being a match and wish you the best." So, before you do the "bless and release," make sure you are sure that's what you want and then stick to it.

Moreover, the concise "bless and release" may be fine in the early stages of dating but may not be enough if the two of you have had a longer and deeper connection. For example, you may want to say a little more than just, "Thanks for being my partner for the past five years. But I am not feeling a romantic connection here. Good luck out there." Your partner might deserve a more elaborate explanation, especially if he or she needs to know what to do with the house and kids that you share, for example.

Nevertheless, when done properly and for the right wrong situation, this "bless and release" approach could be a refreshing release from all the vague, double-speaking game playing that's going on out there in the dating world. And who knows? If the person you are releasing ends up finding the right match for him or her as a result, that person may end up offering blessings for what you did.

item.title: Evil Deeds and Dangerous States of Mind
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

Evil Deeds and Dangerous States of Mind

What are the common factors that cause someone to kill and can it be prevented?

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Convicted killers like Bryan Kohberger are human beings with severe psychiatric problems.
  • If we wish to better comprehend the evil deeds of such criminals, it is essential to study their psychology.
  • Not every person who commits such horrific crimes is necessarily a psychopath or sociopath.
Source: HY-DP/Shutterstock

What compels accused or convicted murderers like Bryan Kohberger, Lindsay Clancy, Luigi Mangione, and Tyler Robinson to kill? Are there any commonalities that can help us to better comprehend their evil deeds? In this part (Part 1) of a series on criminal forensic psychology, let us begin with the deeply disturbing case of Bryan Kohberger.

Mr. Kohberger, a former doctoral student in criminal justice, is currently serving four consecutive life sentences in a maximum security prison after pleading guilty to and being convicted of the horrific killings of four students from the University of Idaho in 2022. (See my prior post.) However, he is now again claiming to be innocent of these murders and seeks to formally withdraw his original 2025 guilty plea claiming it was made under duress and with incompetent legal counsel.

While this appeal, according to legal experts, is highly unlikely to succeed, there is now some information available regarding his psychiatric or mental health history that could shed more light on what might have motivated these extremely evil deeds, thanks to a recently unsealed neuropsychological evaluation conducted for the defense team, which reportedly stated that Kohberger was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, OCD, DCD (developmental coordination disorder, typically associated with ASD), ADHD, ARFIC (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder sometimes associated with anxiety disorders, autism, schizophrenia, and other eating disorders), anorexia nervosa, unspecified depressive disorder, and opioid use disorder now in sustained remission.

I have never personally evaluated nor met Mr. Kohberger, and cannot ethically diagnose him without having done so. But, as a practicing forensic psychologist with extensive experience working with both the criminal and civil courts in California, reading this long laundry list of psychiatric diagnoses, when added to what we already knew about him, paints a clinical picture of someone who has suffered most of their life from severe and chronic anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, chronic depression including extremely low self-esteem compensated for by narcissistic defense mechanisms, and, based on the method and description of the overkill at the bloody murder scene, immense but mostly repressed or unconscious anger, rage, resentment, and embitterment or what one might generically refer to as an "anger disorder."

Here, as in similar cases I have seen over the years, the presence of the repressed anger or rage may be key, since it drives and motivates such ultra-violent behavior. Frequently, the anxiety symptoms, including obsessive-compulsive disorder (which is an anxiety disorder by definition), and depression, can be the consequence of chronic repression of the rage or what I call the daimonic. (See Diamond, 1996; 2025.)

Substance abuse is commonly used by such individuals as a form of self-medication for suppressing and keeping the feelings of anxiety, anger, rage, and depression at bay. Severe and chronic anxiety (and/or depression) can also play a significant and exacerbating role in disorders such as ADHD and mild autism spectrum insofar as they can cause social and cognitive impairment in general, and more specifically, serious deficits in one's capacity to focus, concentrate, and recall information and events, both recent and remote. Sometimes, transient or chronic psychotic symptoms such as command hallucinations or paranoid delusions may be present, though there are, at least thus far, no prior indications of this in the Kohberger case.

However, it has become more clear now, according to this latest report, that Mr. Kohberger suffers from not only some neurological but also severe psychological and emotional problems. But from whence did they spring? Sexual frustration? (Some speculate he was a so-called incel, like mass shooter Elliot Rodger.) Social rejection? Having been bullied as a boy for being morbidly obese or because of his psychiatric symptoms by his peers? Dysfunctional family dynamics? Or, was he simply born this way?

What is conspicuously missing thus far to my knowledge is any meaningful information on Kohberger's family and particularly his relationship with his parents. This, psychologically speaking, is where at least some of the kinds of problems from which he seemingly suffers usually start. (It has been reported that he called his parents, and particularly his mother, repeatedly right after the murders, suggesting some special closeness, connection, or dependency.)

Assuming, for example, that he is indeed a very angry guy, what made Kohberger so mad — mad or enraged enough to kill, no, butcher, four innocent college kids? What happened to him earlier in life? Why was his supposed autism not diagnosed and treated sooner, as these symptoms are usually evident by age 2? He reportedly has two sisters: How did they fare in the family system and how are they functioning now?

How did he feel toward them? (Bizarrely, it seems that one older sister, a former actress, appeared some 15 years ago, while Bryan was still in his teens, in a low-budget slasher film about someone slaughtering young college students. Coincidence?) These unanswered questions are not at all a matter of trying to blame Bryan Kohberger's parents or family for what he did, since that was solely his own responsibility. But answers are essential in better understanding how he went on to become the murderous person he did.

From a strictly diagnostic standpoint, I believe the crucial remaining question for the forensic mental health professionals involved in this case has to do with whether Mr. Kohberger manifests some kind of previously undiagnosed personality disorder, an overarching character structure that unites his seemingly disparate symptoms into some more or less cohesive and enduring pattern of experience and behavior. Based on the limited collateral information publicly available, and my previous clinical experience, I suspect that he may.

The most likely diagnosis in tragic cases such as this usually would be antisocial personality disorder or psychopathy. (See Diamond, 2022.) However, to diagnose APD specifically, there must be documented evidence of "a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, occurring since age 15 ... [and] ... of conduct disorder with onset before age 15" (DSM-5-TR). Based on what we, the public, currently know about Kohberger's history, maybe or maybe not.

Perhaps surprisingly to some, the diagnosis of APD cannot be made simply based on the nature of the evil, heinous, and sadistic crime itself. One need not necessarily be a psychopath or antisocial personality to commit such a violent offense. For instance, horrifying crimes of passion can sometimes be committed by people without any history of antisocial traits. The terrifying fact is that every human being has the capacity for evil, though it is far more comforting to convince ourselves that only some minuscule percentage of the population (an estimated 1%-4% are psychopaths or sociopaths) could conceivably be capable of doing something so exceptionally evil, cruel, and brutal.

So, at this point, more data would be needed before reaching a specific personality disorder diagnosis, though there may, in my view, be sufficient information right now to support the presence in cases such as this of some type of character disorder (e.g., general personality disorder with antisocial traits). If so, such a diagnosis made by the forensic clinicians involved could help us to make a little more sense of who this individual is and why he did what he did.

item.title: Is Greed the Strongest Motivator in Our Society?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Is Greed the Strongest Motivator in Our Society?

Greed precludes the very goals that it’s intended to capture.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Greed begins within a perfectly normal reward system within the brain.
  • “High future discounting” is when the value of a reward decreases the further into the future it's delayed.
  • Dispositional greed is encoded in molecular mechanisms, especially those involving dopamine.

In the political thriller “Scandal,” which aired from 2012 through 2018, the main character, crisis manager Olivia Pope, once exclaimed, “I don’t understand the kind of people who have everything, but still want more.” Although Pope never uses the word greed, her wording fits a commonly employed description of what is, to most people, a maddening and relatively incomprehensible character trait.

Psychological Impact of Greed

Greed can be usefully defined as an insatiable desire for more: wealth, power, or possessions. The key word is insatiable. A unique psychological component of greed, as mentioned by Pope, consists of never being satisfied with what one has, but constantly wanting more. “Dispositional greed” is the psychological term for this tendency over the long-term to want more and more, and to feel dissatisfied with what one already has. Not surprisingly, such an attitude can almost be guaranteed to exact emotional costs: frustration, impulsivity, aggression, and exploitative behaviors, along with their consequences. Controlled studies have also found significant associations between greed and depression, aggression, and detrimental interpersonal relationships accompanied by a general decline in mental health.

These findings on the harmful effects of greed have not so far provided a categorical distinction between normal acquisitiveness and greed. Rather than a clear demarcation, research suggests a continuum involving character traits such as reward seeking, emotional regulation, anticipation, motivation, and appraisals of the future consequences of current behavior. At the one end of the continuum are the vast majority of us, who are comfortable with comparatively modest monetary and material arrangements and who score normally on these character traits.

But at the other end of the continuum—full-blown greed—all parameters clock in at the extremes: excessive reward seeking to the point of monomania coupled with destructive behaviors involving verbal and sometimes even physical aggression. This linkage is referred to as the Frustration Aggression Hypothesis: Unrealized desires segue into dissatisfaction, frustration, and hostility.

Understanding the moral and ethical conundrum posed by insatiable desire is really necessary if one wishes to understand greed, perhaps the strongest motivating factor within our current society.

Insights From Brain Science

Fortunately, current brain research provides some useful insights.

Greed begins with a normal reward system within the brain consisting of a delicate balance between reward evaluation and the cognitive control needed to set limits on how far one will go to get what one wants. Differences in the balance between reward evaluation and cognitive control may help explain why some people are greedier than others and remain so throughout their lives irrespective of consequences. A temporal element also exists. Greed is associated with what psychologists refer to as “high future discounting”: the value of a reward decreases the further into the future it must be delayed. How does this play out in the brain?

The nucleus accumbens, a reward center within the emotion-associated limbic system, is ordinarily balanced by the input from the prefrontal cortex. In the “I want it now!” mode characteristic of greed, the nucleus accumbens is activated out of proportion to the restraining influence of the prefrontal lobes. This translates into a temporal choice where the future is ignored (discounted) in the interest of an excessive and, in many instances, obsessive focus on the present.

There is also a genetic profile of greed. Dispositional greed is encoded in molecular mechanisms, especially those involving the neurotransmitter dopamine. Both dopamine and the genes governing its signaling are linked to impulsivity. Thus, any satisfactory explanation of greed would have to incorporate the distributed neural activity patterns of dopamine along with its underlying molecular mechanisms. But before we move too hastily in that direction, here’s a question:

Based on research so far on the neuroscience of greed, it may be possible in the probably not too distant future to come up with some chemical panacea to reduce greed, a kind of anti-greed pill. But is that goal—the elimination or at least the reduction of greed—necessarily a good thing?

As background for answering that question, consider that greed is not universally spurned but, on the contrary, is idolatrized within certain segments of our society. “Greed, for lack of a better word, is good. Greed is right, greed works,” as ruthless investment speculator Gordon Gekko famously said in the movie Wall Street.

To encounter innumerable examples of the dark side of greed, replay some episodes from the television show “American Greed.” Its 19-year history since its first broadcast in 2007, one year before the financial crisis of 2008, has provided the producers of the show with a deluge of greed stories. “American Greed” regularly features profiles of people with uncontrollable greed participating in investment scams, corporate deception, Ponzi schemes (Bernie Madoff), and mortgage fraud.

Behind all of these varied examples of greed, a transitional common pattern can be discerned: Ambition leads to initial success, followed by an appetite for more and more, leading to deception, rationalization, and a relentless escalation of desire coupled with an inability to control that desire. Many of the people profiled on “American Greed” start off as what most people would consider exemplars of success. Thanks to their ambition and resulting success, they accrue considerable wealth. But that isn’t “enough.” In the further pursuit of riches, they began taking on increasing risks until their obsession with the greater and greater accumulation of wealth results in catastrophic personal consequences ranging from being unmasked to a criminal trial culminating in a lengthy prison term.

Ironically, the psychological cost of uncontrolled greed precludes those very goals that greed is supposedly intended to capture: security, social standing, fulfilled relationships, satisfaction, and happiness.

As an indicator of how greed is currently playing out in the “real world,” consider Proposition 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on the roughly 250 billionaires residing in the state of California. On August 25, 2026, Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google, launched a $90 million spending initiative aimed at defeating the bill. This funding translates into 11,000 times the amount of airtime booked by the tax proponents. But that is not stopping the campaign efforts of a new group, “Tax the Greedy Billionaires,” for whom Proposal 40 is a “story about who has control over our future.”

Where would you place your bet on how this debacle is going to play out? And beyond November, how does one even begin processing, much less reversing, something so pervasive and so powerful as greed?

item.title: Structured Breathing and Substance Use Recovery
item.description:
Addiction

Structured Breathing and Substance Use Recovery

Breath-based meditation practices may support healing from substance use.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Recovery involves retraining the brain, not only overcoming physical dependence.
  • Meditation and breathing may reduce stress, a major trigger for relapse.
  • Structured breathing can support emotional regulation, resilience, and healthier responses to cravings.

Recovery from substance use disorder is often described as a process of breaking physical dependence. Increasingly, research suggests it is also a process of retraining the brain—in other words, overcoming psychological dependence.[1,2,3]

Substance use affects many of the systems responsible for motivation, reward, emotional regulation, stress response, and decision-making. Over time, repeated exposure to drugs or alcohol can alter neural pathways associated with cravings and habit formation, making recovery challenging even after physical withdrawal has ended.[4,5]

Addressing the Underlying Patterns That Contribute to Relapse

Researchers and clinicians are exploring approaches that address not only behavior but also the underlying stress and emotional patterns that contribute to relapse. Among these approaches, meditation and structured breathing practices have gained growing attention.

One reason is their impact on the nervous system.[6,7]

Many individuals in recovery experience heightened stress reactivity. The body becomes conditioned to respond to discomfort, uncertainty, or emotional distress with intense physiological activation. This state can increase cravings and make it more difficult to maintain healthy coping mechanisms.

Meditation and rhythmic breathing practices appear to work in the opposite direction, with one study showing a 52 percent reduction rate in depression via meditation in just eight weeks. By activating the parasympathetic nervous system, they help shift the body out of a chronic fight-or-flight state and into one associated with rest, recovery, and regulation.[6,7]

This shift may be particularly important during recovery. Stress is one of the most commonly reported triggers for relapse, and the ability to regulate stress in real time can influence how individuals respond to cravings, setbacks, and emotional challenges.[4]

Research on Sudarshan Kriya Yoga (SKY Breath), a structured breathing and meditation practice, suggests benefits that extend beyond temporary relaxation. Studies have documented reductions in stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms, as well as improvements in emotional well-being and resilience. These outcomes are relevant because mood disorders and emotional dysregulation frequently coexist with substance use disorders and can complicate recovery.[8]

Effects on Brain Function

The effects may also involve changes in brain function.

Substance use disorders are associated with alterations in areas of the brain involved in impulse control, reward processing, and emotional regulation. Emerging evidence suggests that meditation and breath-based practices can influence many of these same neural networks. Through repeated practice, the brain may become better able to tolerate discomfort, regulate emotions, and interrupt automatic behavioral patterns.[5,6,7]

In practical terms, this means individuals may develop a greater capacity to pause before reacting. The space between a craving and a response can become larger. While this does not eliminate urges altogether, it may strengthen a person's ability to navigate them without returning to substance use.[6,9]

The Role of Connection

Another important component of recovery is connection.

Substance use disorders are often accompanied by isolation, shame, and disconnection from others. Many meditation and breathing programs are delivered in group settings, creating opportunities for shared experience and social support. These environments can help restore a sense of belonging and provide positive reinforcement during a period that is often marked by significant personal change.[10]

Programs such as the SKY Recovery Program have integrated evidence-based breathing techniques, meditation, and community support into recovery settings. Participants frequently report improvements in emotional stability, stress management, sleep quality, and overall well-being. While these approaches are not intended to replace medical treatment, counseling, or recovery programs, they may serve as valuable complementary tools within a broader recovery plan.[1]

Taken together, these findings point toward a broader understanding of recovery.

Recovery is not simply the absence of substance use. It is the process of rebuilding the internal systems that support health, resilience, and choice. Meditation and structured breathing practices may help strengthen those systems by improving emotional regulation, reducing stress, supporting neural recovery, and fostering connection.[11]

In a field that has traditionally focused on managing symptoms and preventing relapse, these practices offer something different: a way to actively cultivate the mental and physiological conditions that make long-term recovery possible.[12]

item.title: A Well-Tended Mind
item.description:
Self-Talk

A Well-Tended Mind

Cultivating greater well-being with awareness and curiosity.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Regular check-ins on yourself and your internal operating system are vitally important.
  • Check in on yourself with more curiosity and less judgment.
  • Use your discoveries and insights to broaden your options for responding.
Source: tara-winstead / Pexels

The mind is an amazing source of information and inspiration, yet, left unattended, it can also cause significant misery. Unfortunately, we rarely give our minds the same level of care we grant other aspects of our lives, even though it has a significant influence over our well-being. We often treat our minds like an appliance or computer inherited long ago, expecting peak performance without regular maintenance, ignoring blinking warning lights that signal a need for repairs or upgrades. The truth is, our internal operating system needs ongoing care if we expect it to function well.

Everything you think, feel, and do is influenced by your state of mind. Certain attitudes, stories you tell yourself, and unaddressed issues simmer just below the surface of our awareness, coloring how you perceive and respond to your experience. This post is your invitation to better understand what's going on in your mind and move into a more intentional relationship with your inner landscape.

Are you able to slow down and investigate when you’re slipping into a troubling state, and can you do so with curiosity rather than judgment? From a place of awareness, we can pause, reflect on our internal state, and consider more skillful ways to process our experience. We can look for support when needed and try to address our concerns in a helpful manner.

Curiosity and Self-Awareness

Curiosity and self-awareness keep our minds from running solely on autopilot—simply reacting and responding without reflection. It is immensely helpful to understand our different states of mind so we can "change the channel" when we find ourselves stuck on a station feeding us unhelpful messages, or when our unsettled state signals that something needs more careful attention.

I, too, need these regular check-ins. Mid-afternoon last Monday, I felt a knot in my stomach, while grumpy thoughts bumped around in my head, signaling the onset of a difficult mood. My patience with my husband had evaporated over a trivial matter, and everything just felt off. The glass seemed half-empty. Before I let my moodiness hijack my entire day or spill over onto anyone else, I stopped and asked myself, “What is going on? What’s got you in such a mood?”

I wasn’t looking for excuses; I was searching for clarity. If I could meet my experience with nonjudgmental curiosity, useful insights might emerge. As I slowed down, it occurred to me: I was recovering from a virus, wrestling with a looming deadline, and still reeling from news of my sister’s recent cancer diagnosis. I wasn’t just “grumpy.” I was physically depleted and carrying the weight of stress and worry I had not yet sufficiently tended to. That brief moment of awareness didn’t erase the diagnosis or the deadline, but it halted the downward spiral before it got any worse. It gave me an opportunity to constructively address what was going on. My mood had meaning. I now had other options.

A Self-Awareness Intervention

If you find your state of mind becoming overly negative or harsh, try this self-awareness intervention:

  • The Pause: Stop what you are doing. Take a deep breath. Slow down. Get curious.

  • The Inquiry: Ask yourself, “What is going on with me? What is troubling me or calling for my attention?” Make space to explore what is contributing to your mood—are you stressed, worried, hurt, frustrated, avoiding something, or dealing with a disappointment?

  • The Compassionate Pivot: Instead of judging your state, offer yourself the same grace you would offer a friend. What might help right now—rest, a boundary, some support, a new attitude, or time to process?

We can’t control the emergence of every thought, feeling, or mood, but we can learn to respond to them with greater awareness and thoughtfulness. Remember to pause and be curious. Respond to what you discover with interest, kindness, and wise action. Tend to your internal operating system with the attention it deserves, just as you would for other important aspects of your life. As Ralph Waldo Emerson reminds us:

“What lies before us, and what lies behind us, are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.”

item.title: The Hidden Obstacles to Transformation
item.description:
Mindfulness

The Hidden Obstacles to Transformation

Change itself may not be complicated, but resistance to change often is.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • Resistance to change is often stronger than the desire to change.
  • Awareness is the foundation of lasting transformation.
  • Genuine change occurs when insight is translated into behavior.
Source: Dilock / Adobe Stock

“Change is hard, you go first” –Dilbert

There’s an old story told in psychotherapeutic circles about a man who, suffering from severe flu symptoms, seeks a friend’s advice. The friend rushes over and finds him in a sorry state. His response is simple and direct: “You need to see a doctor and get a prescription before you get worse.” Taking his friend’s advice, the man goes to the doctor and leaves with great hope, carrying a prescription. Unfamiliar with modern medicine, he places the prescription on the kitchen counter, where he can see it every day. He is confused and saddened when his symptoms worsen. Believing he has misjudged the prescription’s power, he moves it to the nightstand beside his bed. Still, he does not improve. Two days later, his friend stops by and finds him extremely ill. Seeing the prescription on the nightstand, the friend asks, “Didn’t you get that filled?” With tears in his eyes, the man responds, “Filled?”

One of the unusual titles given to mental health professionals is “agent of change.” Early in my career, I found this a fitting description because I was trained to help people make healthy changes in their lives. Before long, however, I realized a simple truth: most people do not come to therapy to change; they come to feel better. If therapy does not deliver that relief, they may change therapists instead, seeking someone who will affirm that they are suffering and deserve a better life.

There are many reasons why even people who genuinely seek change become frustrated in their efforts. Many who come to therapy are also trying practices such as yoga, meditation, bibliotherapy, medication, massage, and biofeedback, yet they still find their old patterns stubbornly in control.

Psychotherapy can produce two profound moments with very different outcomes. The first is the “aha!” moment, when something clicks, the client gains insight into the work ahead, and that insight propels them forward. The second is the “uh-oh” moment, when the client realizes that, after listening patiently to stories of pain and suffering, the therapist is going to ask what the client is willing to do differently. This realization can lead someone to withdraw from therapy and later tell friends or loved ones, “I tried therapy. It didn’t work.”

When I reflect on my own struggles, I feel deep empathy for those who want to change how life feels, only to discover that some part of them is resisting the process.

Barriers to Change

Spiritual teacher Jiddu Krishnamurti addressed why people could spend years attending lectures, reading books, and seeking guidance yet remain unchanged. Drawing on his teachings, four common barriers can be summarized:

  1. The preference for comfort over disruption: Fear of the unknown and the desire for security lead many people to remain with what is familiar, even when it is painful, rather than risk the uncertainty of change.
  2. Misunderstanding what change is: We may mistake change for rearranging our lives to fit an ideal. This is sometimes described as redecorating one’s prison cell.
  3. Relying on time and ideals: Many people discover that time alone does not heal every wound. Waiting for relief in an imagined future can prevent action in the present.
  4. Escaping responsibility: One powerful form of resistance is the belief that other people or circumstances are entirely responsible for our current state. Blaming parents, social or political conditions, or economic factors can keep us from taking responsibility for the choices that are ours to make.

Wise teachers have long offered guidance about the path to meaningful change. One familiar saying, often attributed to the Buddha, is: “Do not dwell in the past, do not dream of the future, concentrate the mind on the present moment.”

Change itself may not be complicated, but resistance to change often is. The same mind that wants to change is also the mind resisting change. Something new is therefore needed. As a saying often attributed to Einstein puts it, “We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.”

The Power of Awareness

If this sounds daunting, we still possess a powerful resource for creating lasting change: awareness. When we notice how the mind draws us into unhealthy thought patterns, reinforces self-defeating messages, and turns against us, we begin to loosen its grip on our experience. We come to understand that the mind is not always a reliable guide.

Change begins to move in a new direction when we recognize that not every thought deserves our attention. We can learn to move around troubling thoughts as we would move through a crowd. We can watch them pass like traffic without climbing aboard.

In the end, filling the prescription can begin with one simple practice:

Three times each day, pause and ask yourself:

  • What am I thinking?
  • What am I feeling?
  • What do I need right now?
